1824458,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.8.1.1.2,1956-01-26,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Inquiries of the Ministry finance to study health insurance questions. This committee has been meeting here this week in camera, in accordance with the expressed desire of the provincial representatives at the conference.

I made a public statement of the general policy of the government on this subject at the opening of the conference in October. This has been furnished to all hon. members in the proceedings of the conference. The main point of that policy statement was that when a majority of the provincial governments, representing a majority of the people of Canada, are ready to put into effect programs to provide hospital care as a measure of health insurance under provincial jurisdiction and management, the federal government would recommend to parliament legislation to provide financial support and technical assistance to the provinces for such programs.

Constitutional responsibility in this field lies, of course, with the provincial governments, and we have no desire to interfere in their exercise of it, nor to urge any provincial government to take this major step in social policy before it feels prepared to meet the substantial administrative and financial problems which are involved. Provincial spokesmen have made quite clear, however, that they would expect parliament to provide some share of the finances required by a grant in aid, as was done in the case of other major social security and health programs.

Public opinion appears to support the view that it would be proper for the federal government to recommend such assistance. The government has not felt it could rec-omtnend assistance for only a few provinces to undertake this great social innovation, but if a majority of provinces, such as I have mentioned, are ready to embark upon it, and wish assistance, we feel it would be justified.

The discussions with the provincial representatives have now reached a stage where it seems desirable that the federal government should state the nature of the financial assistance it would ask parliament to provide under the circumstances I have described. This is desirable in order that provincial governments can estimate the amounts they would have to finance in undertaking a program along these lines.

I think it is appropriate that I inform the house, in general terms, of the nature of the proposed basis of assistance at about the same time that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, in an adjoining room, is informing the provincial representatives.
He will be reporting in more detail upon these matters to the house at the first appropriate opportunity.

When a majority of the provinces, as I have mentioned, are ready to proceed we would recommend to parliament that it enact legislation to provide a grant to each province operating a hospital care insurance program. The amount of the grant would be a fraction of carefully defined shareable operating costs of hospital care, being 25 per cent of the per capita shareable costs in that province, plus 25 per cent of the average per capita shareable costs in Canada as a whole, multiplied by the population covered by the provincial program. The programs in which we would share would provide standard ward care.

This formula will leave a substantial incentive for economy and efficiency with each provincial authority, together with a large measure of federal assistance and equity in its distribution. It will mean that on the whole the federal treasury would bear about one-half of the net shareable operating costs of such programs of hospital insurance.

We would not propose under this legislation to share the costs of care for mental illness and tuberculosis, which provincial governments have traditionally provided and for the improvement of which parliament has already been providing grants under the national health grants program.

We are also prepared to include in our recommendation to parliament the addition to this hospital program of laboratory, radiological and other diagnostic services for patients outside of hospitals as well as in them. Already a start has been made toward these services under the national health grants program, and those who have studied the subject consider the provision of these diagnostic services to be a desirable step to take either before or along with a program of insurance for hospital care.",,,,

Pearson (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,CRIMINAL LAW,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,STATEMENT ON SHIPMENT OF ARMS TO EGYPT,Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) asked whether in the shipment of spare parts of world war II type tanks which in his understanding were included in the shipments to Egypt

he was mistaken in this understanding-included any breech blocks. Later on he asked whether in approving the sale of spare parts of world war II type tanks to Egypt the government had taken into consideration the fact that the British tanks which found their way to Egypt via Belgium were complete except for breech blocks.
I assured the house yesterday that in any decisions pertaining to the export of arms from Canada all relevant factors were taken into consideration. With the permission of

Inquiries of the Ministry the house I should now like to amplify that answer, particularly in order to correct the misconception which the hon. member for Eglinton appeared to be labouring under, as reflected in his question.

In the statement I made on January 24 I gave the figures for arms exports to Egypt and to the other states in the Middle East. I explained that the Harvard trainers and spare parts were responsible for practically the whole of the Egyptian figure. I went on to say that the main items covered by the other figures in the report included tracks and spare parts for world war II type tanks. These tank parts were not authorized for shipment to Egypt, as the hon. member assumed. I wish to make clear now that the parts for world war II type tanks to which I referred were not destined for Egypt. I would also wish to add that the lists of such parts as were approved for export included no breech blocks.

,Liberal,,Lester Bowles Pearson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f&Language=E&Section=ALL

Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,CRIMINAL LAW,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,STATEMENT ON SHIPMENT OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT TO SOUTH AMERICA,Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a question asked yesterday of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). The Prime Minister has asked me to answer the question. The question was as follows:
Have any supplies of' military equipment been sent to any South American country in the last two years?

The answer is, no permits were issued for guns, ammunition, or military weapons of any kind, or for military aircraft or military vehicles to South America. A considerable quantity of airframe and aircraft engine spares, and reconditioned engines and parts for military vehicles were export licensed. By no means all of these were necessarily for military use. It should be noted here that since 1954 Canada has become the only source of supply in the western hemisphere for spares for a type of engine in common use in commercial air transport throughout the world, namely the DC-3, and they would be included in those export permits.

The total value of permits issued in 1954 for all South American countries was $119,222, and in 1955 it was $577,231.79. These totals were divided between aircraft spares and vehicle engines and parts as follows: $292,328.29 for aircraft spares; $384,825.50 for vehicle engines and parts.

1824481,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.10.1.5,1956-01-26,ba4bfe17-d7b1-4ef8-9317-f2fea3027bb6,ca.m.7672,Mr. Lesage:,Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources,SAINT JOHN RIVER DEVELOPMENT,INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL CO-OPERATION,,The hon. member did give me notice of his question yesterday, and I have studied the files. I can say that ever since the early plans for further development of power on the upper Saint John river began about ten years ago the federal government has been in close touch with the situation.

The federal government authorized the expenditures that made it possible for the Canadian section of the international joint commission to conduct an exhaustive survey which resulted in 1953 in the comprehensive report ""Water Resources of the Saint John River Basin"". On the basis of this survey the Tobique development has been completed, and the Beech wood project on the main river is now under way by the province.

All the way along there has been a constant exchange of views among provincial and federal technical and financial officials. These discussions appeared to indicate that the development to the end of the Beechwood phase could be carried out by the province of New Brunswick without jeopardizing its credit. It appears, however, that future developments in the province are likely to require additional power on a substantial scale. This larger future development has been represented to the federal government as likely to be beyond the capacity of the province of New Brunswick to finance on its own.

These matters were discussed at the federal-provincial conference last October. At that time it was made clear that provinces were at liberty to submit proposals with respect to provincial development programs, vital to the growth of the province and beyond the financial capacity of the province to bear. While Premier Flemming was here for the conference, we had a meeting together with some of his officials and officials of my department to discuss the power situation in
New Brunswick. Since the conference the premier of New Brunswick has written to the Prime Minister and to me about the subject. In his letter to me Mr. Flemming said:
New Brunswick would like to submit a suitable memorandum in connection with the matter mentioned at an early date.
The letters were dated October 20, 1955. I replied on November 1 saying:
Such a supplementary memorandum from you covering the specific matters you have in mind would be of great assistance to me.

I have no doubt that there have been a great many matters engaging the premier's attention, and I have not as yet received the memorandum to which he referred. I am informed that one of his advisers indicated in a telephone call to one of the officers of my department on January 23 that the memorandum was currently under consideration by the premier, and I have no doubt it will be forthcoming shortly.

,Liberal,,Jean Lesage,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ba4bfe17-d7b1-4ef8-9317-f2fea3027bb6&Language=E&Section=ALL

1824483,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.10.1.7,1956-01-26,ba4bfe17-d7b1-4ef8-9317-f2fea3027bb6,ca.m.7672,Mr. Lesage:,Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources,SAINT JOHN RIVER DEVELOPMENT,INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL CO-OPERATION,,I have said and it has been known for some months that the Beechwood development could be carried out without jeopardizing the credit of the province of New Brunswick. That has been the case and it has been known for some months. Campney (Minister of National Defence):,Minister of National Defence,DIVE BOMBER TRAINING,STATEMENT AS TO USE OF CHIPMUNK AIRCRAFT,,Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet may I refer to two questions that were asked recently. On Tuesday last the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) asked two questions, the first of which was as follows:
Has dive bomber training, as was practised during world war II with Harvard aircraft, been discontinued or is it still continued as part of the training program?
The answer to that question is that dive bombing training as conducted during world war II was discontinued in the Royal Canadian Air Force in February, 1954.
The hon. member's second question was:
Has the Chipmunk aircraft not replaced the Harvard aircraft as a primary trainer?

In answer to that question I may say that, under arrangements now being introduced, Royal Canadian Air Force pilot trainees receive their first flying training on Chipmunk aircraft, but they still train later on Harvards in order to complete their basic training, so the Chipmunk cannot be said to have superseded or replaced the Harvard. Rather, it supplements it.

Campney (Minister of National Defence):,Minister of National Defence,REPORTED USE OF BUTTER IN MILITARY ESTABLISHMENTS,,,Yesterday, on the orders of the day, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) asked whether margarine has been or is being extensively used in military establishments. The answer is no. The tri-service ration scale provides for the use of butter, a two-ounce ration per man per day, and does not provide for the use of margarine at all. Consequently, supply officers do not purchase and supply depots do not maintain any stocks of margarine.

What I have just said applies only to food supplies purchased by public funds. 1824564,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.25.1.1,1956-01-26,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. H. R. Argue (Assiniboia) moved,,SMALL LOANS ACT,AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR A REDUCTION IN RATE OF INTEREST,,the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Small Loans Act.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to reduce the maximum rate that may be charged by small loan companies from 24 per cent to 12 per cent per annum. I believe the prevailing rate of 24 per cent per annum is fantastic, exorbitant and unnecessary and that it should be reduced. I moved a similar bill in this house last year and I was amazed at the amount of support the proposition I moved at that time received from one end of the country to the other. I think I can safely say that I have never proposed a bill or any other measure that received such widespread support. The support was not only prevalent throughout the country but I find it has been quite general amongst members of this house.

I hope that we shall have a good discussion of this bill this afternoon so that the government will be able to learn the position of various hon. members and the position of the various parties in relation to the bill, and may use that information when it brings down an amendment to the Small Loans Act which I venture to hope will result in a substantial reduction in interest rates.

There are other amendments I might also have suggested to the Small Loans Act. The present ceiling on interest rates applies to loans up to $500. Certainly the purchasing power of a $500 loan in 1955 is very small compared to the purchasing power of a $500 loan in 1939 when the Small Loans Act was last amended. I might have suggested that the ceiling be raised from $500 to $1,500 or $2,000 but I have found previously that when a private member puts more than one idea in

a bill very frequently another hon. member, who for some reason or other is desirous of opposing the bill, will latch on to one part of the bill and indicate that if that one point were not there he would support the bill and that as far as the other part of the bill is concerned he is all for it. Therefore I have limited this bill to the simple proposition that an interest rate of 12 per cent should be the limit of interest charged by small loan companies. I have on the order paper another bill which I allowed to stand today which contains the proposition that interest charges throughout the country on all other credit should not exceed 12 per cent per annum.
As I said, I think an interest rate of 24 per cent per year is fantastic. I think it is incredible that in a country as economically strong as Canada a great many people-yes,

I would even say millions of working Canadians-have to accept loans and credit bearing an interest rate or charge of 24 per cent. These high rates are not confined to loans advanced by small loan companies alone. Extremely high rates are charged by finance companies when one finances an automobile, a television set or some other item. Finance companies, however, as X have been able to find out, do not necessarily charge the highest rates that are charged on credit advanced in this country. Some of the greatest offenders in so far as the rates they charge are concerned are the big mail order houses. On the smallest purchase on their budget plans, Simpson's and Eaton's levy the fantastic charge of 54 per cent. It is true that as the amount of the instalment purchase increases the rate goes down but it goes down to only 15 or 18 per cent a year, depending on the type of item that is purchased.

From time to time I have read accounts of the interest rates that are charged in other countries. I have heard hon. members in this house refer to the exorbitant interest rates that used to be charged in nationalist China. On one occasion I heard an hon. member say that interest rates in that country having been allowed to go to 50 per cent or more contributed to the cause that resulted in the subsequent revolution in that country. I remember my personal reaction in the past when I read of these high interest rates in other countries. I said to myself, ""I am glad I am living in Canada where such interest rates are seldom charged""; but after having seen the practice of small loan companies, finance companies and mail order houses in Canada I discovered that many rates charged here are almost as high. For that reason I am proposing that the house consider imposing a limitation of 12 per cent on such charges.

The Canadian who is financially well off and who has a high income does not have the same need for credit as the ordinary working Canadian. The former can go to a bank and borrow money at 6 per cent or perhaps 5 per cent without much trouble. The ordinary working people of this nation, regardless of whether they live in the city or on farms, are often required to pay fantastic rates when they borrow money or finance purchases. The legislation we now have is in effect class legislation and constitutes class distinction. It means that the people in low income groups who from time to time have the greatest need for credit are forced to pay exorbitant interest rates because of the laws of this country. I believe that any progressive democracy, any civilized nation, should take steps periodically tc reduce the general rate of interest and tc allow the ordinary working people of the country to obtain credit at reasonable rates

In certain fields credit has been providec at reasonable rates by government legislation. We have a National Housing Act whicl enables a great many people to own theii own homes, paying an interest charge of 51 per cent. That is good legislation. We hav< the Farm Improvement Loans Act, whicl is another example, under which farmer! can obtain credit at a rate of 5 per cent That, too, is good legislation. There is, how ever, a vast field in which the people wh< must obtain credit have to pay the exorbitan interest rates I mentioned.

The amount of credit available in thi country is steadily increasing. I have in m; hand the latest Bank of Canada statistica summary which lists the amount of outstand ing credit as at 30 September, 1955, a follows: Ordinary charge accounts $535 mil lion, instalment credit through retail $30 million, instalment credit through financ companies $578 million, cash personal loan $790 million, a total credit of $2,212 millior If one made the assumption-and this migh not be a good assumption-that each out standing credit item amounted to a rathe large sum, let us say $1,000, then thes statistics show that 2,212,000 Canadians hav obtained credit of one kind or another. Th sum of $2,212 million in outstanding credi is just twice as high as it was four year before. I think we will all agree that in th future Canadians are going to use more an more credit; as our nation develops, as ou country expands, the need for credit wi increase. Therefore the value that will resu from the step I am suggesting will b enormous today and will have even greats benefit as years go by.
I believe that the parliamentary assistar to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benidicksor

the federal government has had to pay out of the amount of its guarantee under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, %30 of the total guarantee. In other words, the amount that has been paid up to date is almost negligible. I wish to point out, of course, that all outstanding loans have not yet been paid, but nevertheless I do not think any hon. member of this house will say that when the present loans have been finalized the cost to the government will be anywhere near its total guarantee or, for that matter, will be many more times the very small guarantee that has already been paid.

I believe that 12 per cent is still too high. I know of no reason why ordinary Canadians who want small loans, who want to buy articles of furniture, who want to buy automobiles, who need money to pay doctors' bills or hospital bills, and so on should be charged even the high rate of 12 per cent when statistics and records show that the risk in this field is very small. I would like to see the interest rate at not 12 per cent but six per cent or five percent, the rate that has already been established under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I am suggesting that if necessary the government should be prepared to pass an act parallel to the Farm Improvement Loans Act-it might be called a family welfare loans act-under which the federal government might make a 10 per cent guarantee to the banks as it does now under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, with the measure of risk so small that the Canadian Bank of Commerce has set up a reserve for bad debts of just -25 per cent. The government, by such action and by the payment over the years of a very tiny sum of money, would save working Canadians in the future hundreds of millions of dollars and would remove millions of Canadians from the necessity of paying exorbitant charges of 24 per cent to loan companies which themselves are now acting as sharks in the small loan field.

1824586,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.1,1956-01-26,afb82da5-dc00-4466-9d55-760139bf3d12,ca.m.2667,Mr. A. H. Hollingworth (York Centre) moved:,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide national scholarships and bursaries for students at the university level who are in financial need, in so far as the subject matter of this resolution is within the competence of parliament.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I move this resolution. I would hope for support worthy of the motion from all sections of the house. One can observe in this House of Commons hon. members who have played and are still playing a distinguished role in the field of education in Canada. One might mention the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), who is chancellor of Victoria College at the University of Toronto, or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), who has been president of the University of New Brunswick, or the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell), who is chairman of the board of trustees of that noble seat of learning, my own Queen's University. This house is studded with Rhodes scholars and with other scholarship winners and gold medalists. The list is indeed impressive. We have former school teachers and university professors sitting in all sections of the house. I shall therefore assume at the outset that I shall receive a sympathetic hearing.

The purposes of this resolution are twofold; first, to provide financial assistance for students who have embarked, perhaps hazardously and with uncertainty, on a university career, and who might otherwise have to quit their studies for lack of money; second, to enable school graduates to attend university by providing financial assistance.

I should like at the outset to pay tribute to those private members who have in the past spoken on this or allied proposals, and I refer particularly to the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) and the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Fairey), both of whom are distinguished educators. I think all hon. members will attest to the desirability of some form of specific federal assistance, provided that such assistance does not impinge upon the provincial jurisdiction in the field of education.

That, of course, has been the great difficulty with federal aid. It would mean assistance in the general field of education, which is proscribed by our constitution, the British North America Act. It would be unconstitutional, since general education comes

within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, as set out in the said act. That is the reason the federal government cannot provide grants holus-bolus to the provinces for education. For example, the federal government cannot say to the province of Ontario, here is a grant to hard-pressed North York township for its schools.

It follows, therefore, that any aid must not infringe upon or violate or interfere with provincial jurisdiction and control. It would appear that the answer may be found in the fact that although the federal government will not come into the general field of education, nevertheless it is willing and is receptive to assisting in specialized fields as for example, vocational training, D.V.A. student assistance and student aid. The purpose of this resolution today is to discuss a plan for more student aid. That is why I say my resolution is constitutionally unimpeachable, and hence should be acceptable unreservedly even to those who are the most zealous custodians of provincial autonomy.

I will point out to hon. members shortly how legislation in existence at the present time and jointly administered provincially and federally may well be the method of carrying out the request I am raising.

I should like to advance several reasons, Mr. Speaker, why my resolution would be not only desirable but obligatory if this country is to go on to its destiny. It might be desirable, however, at this point to mention briefly why the university is so important to our Canadian way of living.

It is almost unnecessary for one to extol the role of the university in our lives. The university is a force of incalculable good in a technological age. It has played a powerful and important role in shaping the destiny of Canada. The university is one of the founts of freedom. As I see it, the function of the university is to teach its students to think, to probe, to inquire, to elucidate, to inspire. It should be a forum for dissent, if need be, and not a stronghold of uniformity and orthodoxy, for the latter may inexorably snuff out the smouldering coals of creative ideas and thought and endeavour.

Let us be clear at the outset that these bursaries are not for the brilliant students of independent means. Such bursaries and scholarships as I propose would be allembracing for the students who need financial assistance. One readily knows the importance of engineers, scientists and technicians to this great nation, whose mineral potential has scarcely been scratched; whose power resources are limitless both with regard to water and atomic energy and whose manufacturing potential is as yet in its early stages.

I am one who believes that the humanities and the arts are just as important as the sciences. Canadian universities have not neglected the humanities; in fact, I believe our Canadian educational system, of which the universities are an integral part, accounts in part for the maturity of the Canadian people and possibly indicates also why the virulent seeds of McCarthyism with its attendant hysteria and obscurantism have never managed to take root in the Canadian soil.

Many reasons could be cited for the desirability of my resolution. On a large canvas it may be affirmed that greater assistance to needy university students is a priceless investment in young Canadians and in Canada. As the Prime Minister said at McMaster University on October 20, 1955, when he received the honorary degree of doctorate of laws: The object of higher education and especially education in the arts and humanities is to teach us to think clearly. At no time in history has it been so important to think clearly when man's ability to destroy himself seems at times to have outstripped his ability to solve the problems which arise between him and his fellow men.

The whole concept was tried out on a large scale with D.V.A. students after the war. It worked magnificently. Many went into universities and the professions who would not have otherwise been able to do so. I dare say there are quite a number of such graduates in this house today.

The economic and financial barrier of education restraining many who were financially embarrassed was swept away. An interesting study at the University of Toronto revealed that the servicemen who passed through Varsity cut across all social and economic groups; and education, which ordinarily was for the families of wealth and for those from the professional and mercantile groups, was extended to those from the families of skilled, semi-skilled and even unskilled workers. Truly this was democracy in action.

The D.V.A. program was expensive, very expensive; from 1942 to 1955 somewhere in the neighbourhood of $220 millions were spent for vocational and university training, or an average of over $16,900,000 per year. I do not know how much of this sum was expended in assisting students through university. What I do know, however, is that it did not take the Department of National Revenue too long to collect this sum in income taxes from D.V.A. graduates. It certainly follows that revenue from personal income taxes will be greatly increased as more university graduates go out into Canadian life. University graduates become the architects, the engineers, the doctors, the dentists, the lawyers and are now sought for executive positions in industry. This scheme

therefore makes admirable sense from a national investment point of view. The federal government is vitally interested in the training of university personnel. Hon. members will note the number of top notch civil servants employed in government service and in important research bodies like the national research council, for example, who are university graduates.

It would appear that university education is practically necessary for almost any form of personal advancement and indeed, as I say, must be freely available if the best qualified are to hold key positions in Canadian society. At the present time stringent financial barriers do exist. Principal James of McGill University pointed out that in 1952 only 3 per cent of Canadian youth attended universities in Canada whereas 15 per cent attended universities in the United States. An editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of January 23, 1956, states that the Canadian university population has now increased to 7-2 per cent. In Australia students registered in degree granting courses in 1952 numbered 21,005 and of this number 7,000, or 33 per cent, received government aid. When one compares the Canadian average with the average in these other countries our position really is shocking. Canada is, I believe, the fourth largest trading nation in the world; we are proud, and justly so, of our national development. Our voice, our opinions, are respected in the councils of the world. And yet it appears that the Canadian university student is certainly the underprivileged legatee of our nation's most cherished traditions. Mr. Speaker, this imbalance must and will be corrected. A large number of those students who do attend Canadian universities live in the town or city where the university is located.

I had an interesting experience recently in this connection. I attended commencement exercises at one of the collegiate institutes in my riding and found that a majority of the graduates were attending university. On making further inquiries of one of the teachers I found out that these young men and women were able to attend university because they lived at home. This surely points out the need for assistance to those who do not live in a university city or town. Dr. Sidney Smith, president of the University of Toronto, put it very succinctly on January 21, 1955, when he said ""It will be increasingly difficult for the boy in Swastika and Sioux Lookout to enroll, as a result of the latest fee increase. It will be a tragedy if universities become places where only the students who live near them are able to attend.""
It has been pointed out that other students who attend university subsequently leave for
reasons that are basically financial, and here you might include those who fail because of the strain of doing full-time work at the same time as studying.

Without doubt there has recently been a substantial increase in the number of students who are attending university. The national federation of Canadian university students, whose efforts have been tireless and even magnificent in promoting bursaries, represents over 50,000 students at more than 20 Canadian universities. Officials of this body informed me that a sum averaging from $1,000 to $1,200 is required to pay for fees and board and room for a year's attendance at a Canadian university or graduate school. As a student is unlikely to earn more than $600 in the summer season, it would seem imperative that the bursaries range in amount from $300 to $500. At the present time most bursary aid is rarely available in amounts of more than $250, and even this is high.

I stated earlier that the federal government is willing to assist in specialized and special fields. I should like to point out to hon. members that vocational training is now consolidated under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, which is broken down into four agreements with the provinces for sharing costs under this act. The act, of course, is administered by the federal Department of Labour. The agreements are as follows: (1) vocational correspondence course agreements,

column2: the vocational schools assistance agreement, and (4) the vocational training agreement. The latter is broken down into training for the disabled, for the armed services, for the unemployed employables, and student aid. In this resolution I am concerned with the latter. The vocational training agreements were allocated $1,342,000 in 1954, out of which student aid received only $309,000. The allocation is still frozen at this amount. The total training program which I have cited above received an appropriation of $4,300,000 in 1954 and the percentage student aid received therefore is only about 7 per cent. My submission would be of course that this student aid should be increased substantially.

column1: I mentioned that conceivably the present system could be enlarged upon. I think it is indeed unfortunate that it was not generally known that there is a system already in existence which is producing splendid results within its limitations. How does the present system then work with regard to student aid? Briefly, the federal government gives direct aid to students through a federal-provincial board called a selection committee. Students are selected by this committee made

up of representatives of the provincial department of education with one member representing the federal Department of Labour. The provincial department of education would of course have a majority control of this board.

For example, I have ascertained that in the province of Ontario the provincial representatives number seven whereas there is but one member representing the federal government. At the discretion of the province help may be given in the form of either a loan or a grant. For example, the provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba and Saskatchewan give loans only, while Ontario and Newfoundland give outright grants with Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec giving both.

The amount of assistance given to an individual may vary from province to province, but in most cases it ranges from $100 to $300. I have some interesting figures from my own province of Ontario. I understand that for the academic year 1954-55 the sum of $316,000 has been spent on bursaries, of which $216,000 came from the provincial government and $100,000 from the federal government through the Department of Labour.

The number of students receiving bursaries was 1,791 out of 2,860 applicants, or 62 per cent. Many of the 1,069 applicants who did not receive bursaries I am informed did not have the requisite 66 per cent academic standing. I have no information available as to the amounts of individual grants, but I understand that for the year 1955-56 the amount of $420,000 will be available, with $100,000 of this amount coming from the federal government.

This joint effort is to be highly commended and it is my plea today that the federal government substantially increase its share so that the joint effort may be considerably extended. This method also shows clearly how federal and provincial governments can work together amicably for the good of Canada. I repeat that the controlling interest here is with the provinces. I would go further and say that this system is forging a great weapon of national unity.
This would seem to me to be the most effective way of handling this whole problem. I am purposely not stating arbitrarily how much money is needed. I am informed that

column2: university students need assistance and I would think that the student aid allocation would have to be at least doubled to $600,000 for a start. But I ask, when one thinks of the incalculable value accruing from this enormously successful venture in education,

column1: in what other way can Canadians get such a good return on their national investment? The answer is obviously nowhere else.

I want to raise the question of assistance by industry and by privately-endowed organizations and foundations. We have noted that in the United States the national merit scholarships corporation has contributed over $20 million for scholarships and bursaries. Of course we have not anything comparable to that in Canada, but I think one should note the splendid work the Atkinson foundation fund has done in this regard.

An editorial in the Toronto Star dated Friday, November 11, 1955, pointed out that the foundation, which has done such magnificent work in the humanities, has helped more than 1,500 Ontario students obtain a university education which otherwise might have been denied to them by a lack of funds. At the end of 1955 contributions were to have reached $393,500. The bursaries, called entrance bursaries, ranged from $200 to $400. This is most commendable, but we must face the fact that there are no other Atkinson foundations.

Of course we should be thankful to such organizations as the I.O.D.E. Mrs. R. C. Bennett of Hamilton, educational convener for the I.O.D.E., stated on October 20, 1955, that for 1955 the I.O.D.E. awarded bursaries totalling $3,700 to college students, and interest free loans totalling $1,100. This fine organization is to be congratulated upon the splendid work it has done in this regard.

Business is becoming aware of the problem but, as President Sidney Smith of the university of Toronto pointed out last week, industry has not been fully cognizant of its responsibility in this regard. Perhaps in all fairness it should be pointed out that the income tax provisions are not conducive to assistance by industry in connection with this matter. No, I think that at the present time this problem can be handled only by the government.

It will be argued that we should not distribute more scholarships until we have more facilities available, and that brings up the related topic of federal assistance to universities generally. It may be asked, why cannot the federal government assist universities in financing of capital assets such as new buildings, laboratories, halls, libraries and so on. As a matter of fact the estimates of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) indicate that unconditional grants to Canadian universities will be approximately $7-8 million for 1955-56. I say with respect that this would appear to be woefully inadequate even for the immediate future.
At the present time there are between

it is estimated that in ten years there will be from 100,000 to 135,000 university students. To confirm these figures one does not have to look any further than the township of North York in which my riding is located. I am informed that in 1960 there will be approximately 81 public schools in the township of North York. Now this is the shocker. In 1960 the township of North York, with an estimated population of 250,000, will have approximately as many schools as are now located in the city of Toronto proper with a static population of 750,000 people.

Let us look at the high school situation in North York. It is estimated that in 1960 there will be approximately 13,000 pupils. Is it any wonder, on the basis of this isolated example, that an estimate of 135,000 university students in 1966 seems to this observer at least to be conservative.

Therefore it appears to me that the federal government should now consider the setting up of a royal commission to study how much money should and could be allocated and dispersed to universities over a long-term period without of course there being any infringement upon provincial autonomy. If the money were allocated directly to the university this surely would not violate provincial sensibilities.
I should like to conclude my remarks in French as I am most anxious to have the support of my French-Canadian colleagues on both sides of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I would not like to miss this opportunity of saying a few words in French to my French-speaking fellow citizens and more particularly to those of my colleagues who represent Quebec constituencies.
I would ask them to support this resolution of mine. I sincerely think that it is one of the best means of promoting national unity in Canada.

Before introducing and explaining my resolution, I want to make it clear that I am among those who recognize that the provinces have competent jurisdiction in the field of education. That is the case in the province of Ontario as well as in all the provinces which stand guard jealously over their rights in the field of education.

I know that French Canadians are proud of their language, their customs and their traditions. They are right in feeling as they do, and I congratulate them on that score. In order to maintain this character, French Canadians mean to keep control of education, in so far as it concerns them. I recognize that fact, as indeed my resolution shows. 1 am also convinced that most Canadians
French and English-speaking, recognize it too.

Of course, my resolution agrees with that principle. There now exists grounds for agreement, a way to get the federal and provincial governments to co-operate in this field of assistance to education. This federal provincial co-operation has already been successful and I believe that more liberal subsidies could now be distributed if the same method were used, that is to say by appointing a selection committee whose task would be to select the students who are in need of money to undertake, continue or complete their studies. This committee would include representatives of the provincial department of education, a representative of the federal government and a representative of the university concerned. Subsidies would be paid directly to the student who would have previously satisfied the said committee as to his genuine financial need. Hon. members will note, Mr. Speaker, that the province would exercise supervision over all the proceedings and maintain its authority. Then, that being the case, there could be no question of federal intervention into provincial affairs.

I say that such a policy is a major factor, not only for needy students, but for Canada as a whole. It is a policy of good understanding, a further step to national unity. We must encourage and multiply contacts and exchanges between French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians. I contemplate a brighter future for the time when there are more exchanges of students, students who will think, first and foremost, as Canadians.

I can assure French Canadians that the people of Ontario want to be their friends. Let me recall, in evidence, that many of the hon. members for Toronto, including the members for Trinity (Mr. Carrick), for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), for Broadview (Mr. Hees), lave made French speeches in this house.

Canada, our beloved Canada, is a bilingual country; a country with two cultures, one Trench, the other English. Are we not going ;o march forward hand in hand in order to make Canada the home of tolerance and of iberalism in its art as well as in its lumanity? My resolution is an appeal to lational unity, along with the respect of the ights and privileges of everyone.
