Drew (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, as on earlier occa-ions, it will be our intention to support the rnrpose of this resolution.
We have had many opportunities to express >ur belief that the plan of scholarships, IMr. Hollingworth.]

which has already worked very satisfactorily through the co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, should be widely extended. We are not dealing with something that is in the realm of vague experiment. Actually there have been scholarships for a great many years, as has been pointed by the mover of this motion. The arrangements have been such that the provincial authorities have had a wide measure of responsibility for the details in this matter. For some time I had some administrative responsibility in connection with the operation of these scholarship arrangements. I know from my own experience that they work satisfactorily. I can recall no single occasion where any serious difficulty presented itself in carrying out those arrangements for scholarships and grants.

The purpose of this motion, undoubtedly, is to emphasize the need for an extension, a very substantial extension, of the award of scholarships to those who seek the opportunity to take advantage of the educational facilities that our universities afford. This can be done without in any way interfering with the exclusive jurisdiction over education which rests with the provincial governments under our constitution. This can undoubtedly be worked out on a satisfactory basis of effective co-operation between the federal and provincial governments.

I am not going to examine in detail the wording of this resolution. The purpose is clear. The purpose is to extend a system of scholarships which will widen the opportunity for young Canadians in every part of Canada, whatever their financial position may be, to avail themselves of the higher educational opportunities that our universities afford.

There are added reasons at this time why all of us should encourage the extension of opportunity at the universities. It is not only the advantage of the young people that is involved-and that is fundamental and vital. What is also involved in the consideration of this subject is the advancement and the strength of the future character of Canada itself. In a large measure, the kind of life that will be lived in our country will be shaped and guided by those who have the advantage of university education and from the pulpit and elsewhere convey those ethical and religious standards which have been the foundation of our life and which we trust will be the foundation of the life of this country in the years ahead.

We must never overlook the fact that, while it is not from university graduates alone that we must seek advancement of the general welfare of our country, one of the fundamental purposes of our universities is to

train people how to live and in turn to pass on the advantage of that training to others. A great part of our university instruction is devoted to the education of teachers themselves. Certainly in that field every encouragement should be offered.

Then there is the field of engineering and scientific skill that is so important at a time when it is so much a part of the great effort that we are making throughout the free world to maintain the strength of our free system. It surely must be a matter of concern to all Canadians and all people of the western world when we find a man, as careful in his statements as Sir Winston Churchill, telling us only within the past few weeks that from the information it has been possible to obtain Soviet Russia is outstripping us in the training of engineers and others with technical knowledge who are so necessary in this period when the great issue between these two different ways of life is being resolved.

Therefore, while it is vitally important that we remember the needs of the young people, while it is vitally important that we bear in mind that every young Canadian who is capable of using the opportunity to have higher education should have that opportunity if possible, we are also dealing with the building of our national strength at a time when national strength is part of the great struggle in which we are engaged. Having regard to the enormous sums of money that are spent on the common effort to build our military strength, it would take a relatively small portion thereof to extend on a very broad basis the kind of technical education, the kind of education in the specialized skills that is needed today. I think we would be serving the dual purpose of widening the opportunities for our youth and building the strength of our nation at the same time.

What happens in the United Kingdom, the United States or in any other free country will be the decision of the governments and elected bodies of those countries. Here our responsibility is for what takes place in Canada. To the extent that this resolution presents the proposition that we should seek a system of scholarships that will encourage young people to go to university, and widens their opportunity to have university courses, we certainly support this effort. To the extent also that this can be done in a way that will guide young people into those special branches of training where graduates are particularly needed at this time, we certainly should encourage the purpose embodied in the resolution.
I have stated before that I believe this can be done without in any way interfering with

provincial authority under our constitution. I have seen it work satisfactorily. I have participated in the actual administration of funds of a similar nature. I know it can be done and therefore I am very happy to support the purpose of the resolution.

Mr. F. T. Fairey (Vicloria, B. C.) Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure to lend my support to the resolution. In fact I rise with some eagerness because on other occasions I have had the pleasure of putting forward the same idea in this chamber. Let me say at once that it is my purpose to form the core of my remarks around what has been so well said by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). The resolution suggests that emphasis be placed upon the need for larger funds to be made available for higher education through the schedule of the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, which has been in effect for 17 years. In those seventeen years the federal government has spent approximately $3 million in co-operation with all the provinces of Canada to provide scholarships and bursaries to young people of high intellect whose economic situation will not allow them to proceed to a school of higher learning.

The subject has been very well covered by my colleague, the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth). He emphasized particularly the need for university training, and I should like to add one or two reasons to those he gave by way of support for a continuation of the schedule but with greatly enhanced facilities both material and financial. In those 17 years the province of British Columbia has sent to various faculties of universities of one kind and another some

column2: students. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, his province, my province and every other province have added funds of their own to those supplied by the federal government. For some years now the federal government has provided about $30,000 in British Columbia. The British Columbia government has matched this amount and added another $100,000 to it for additional loans. The other provinces have done the same thing.

column1: I mention that only to show that there is a realization of the need. What has always appalled me is the waste of intellect and ability of our young people that goes on in our schools. I say that because there are so many people who think that all those who have the ability to proceed to schools of higher learning have the opportunity to do so. I think we all know that financial ability is not always paralleled by intellectual ability. There are thousands of young people

with intellectual ability who have no opportunity whatever to go forward. I have felt for many years that we should do more about it and I hope before I sit down to propose a plan which has some reasonable prospect of success.

I was intrigued by a remark made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) before he left on his trip to Russia. He, of course, comes from my province and, if I may say so, I once had the pleasure of teaching him. He said he was hoping to see the universities in Russia because rumour had it that they were crowded with students. He said he had heard-and he believed it-that the method of selection was as one would expect in a totalitarian society, where they had young people, young men particularly, in the armed services. They had a wonderful opportunity to select those with ability and without any question about it they would simply say to one individual, ""You go to university""; to another, ""You go to technical school"", and to another to go somewhere else. In other words, they had the opportunity to pick out those who could profit by further training and contribute particularly to the technical advancement of their own country.

In Canada today we claim great prosperity, particularly in the industrial field. During the last session of parliament I made a plea for a realization of the shortage we have in this country and I asked this question. If Canada is to progress in the industrial field and in the scientific field, where are we going to get our engineers? What are we doing about training them? Where are we going to get our technicians and what are we doing about training them?

Only the other day during the recess a personnel man of a large industry told me that he had gone to the University of British Columbia-as had others to all universities -recruiting graduates of the faculty of applied science. He said, ""I hoped to get ten for my firm and I obtained only two"". Only the other day in Ottawa an official of the federal government-I should not mention the particular department because I do not think he expected to be quoted-told me that they were going around to universities recruiting. Recruiting what? Recruiting the bright young men now in the universities and offering them jobs. There is a tremendous shortage of engineers and of technicians, particularly in the field of electronics.

How many schools are there in Canada capable of training technicians, particularly in that field which I have mentioned, namely electronics? There is one. It is the Ryerson Institute of Technology in Toronto. There are good technical schools but they are
mostly trade schools. We have one in Vancouver, one in Calgary, one in Winnipeg and there are one or two others. However, they are chiefly trade schools.

Here in my hand I have a letter from the principal of the Ryerson Institute of Technology who is a personal friend of mine. He wrote to me after my address of last session. In his letter he said this:
As you know, the original aim of the Ryerson Institute was to prepare its students to become engineering technicians and over two-thirds of our enrolment is in such courses.
This letter was written in April of last year. He said:
We have now an enrolment of 1,600 in our day classes and 5,200 in the evening school.
Farther on in his letter he said this:

The programs of study for the engineering technicians are based on the assumption that upon graduation their general and theoretical education should reasonably approximate that of a second year university student.

What I want to point out is this, Mr. Speaker. Despite the fact that we have a shortage of professional engineers and of those who design and of those who formulate plans, they are useless unless we have those who have in their hands and in their minds the skill to put those plans into effect. The technician is the important cog in the wheel; and the technician must be guided by those whom we call, for want of a better term, superintendents or foremen or lead hands. Here we have one institution in Canada that is fitted to do that job. Yet at the same time we claim to be growing by leaps and bounds as an engineering and industrial nation.

I said that I was going to suggest a scheme. It may not have any merit, but I think it has. For some years now we have had what is called the vocational training advisory council. I was a member of it. That body meets from time to time. It is supposed to survey the situation throughout the country in the vocational and technical field. It is composed of educators, representatives of industry, of unions-that is of labour-and of the business field. That council is supposed to present recommendations to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), whose department is responsible in this field, in the hope that they may be accepted and be put into effect. I know that for years all we did was to ask for more money. That is a rather common practice of commissions. I am not too happy about the suggestion for a royal commission made by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hol-lingworth). We have had too many of them suggested, and they take too long. We have a body which, in my opinion, is capable of doing this job.

If we are going to tap the resources which we know are in this country, we could enlist the support of the educational administrators across this country. By that I mean the high school principals, the superintendents of education. We could ask them to do just one simple thing, namely to keep their eyes and their ears open for bright students in their schools and to earmark them. If-and I know it could be done-these youngsters could be discovered, watched and then guided in the proper channel, as their abilities would indicate, with the assurance that the federal government, in co-operation with their own educational authorities, would see to it that they had the opportunity to proceed and to develop those abilities which they have displayed, in that way I think we could ensure to every child in Canada with intellectual ability or special skill that he could be of use to himself, be happy in his own work and be of value to his community.

I would suggest to the minister that this problem be thrown into the lap of this vocational training advisory council, with the instruction that they should study this problem of the utilization of the wastage in the intellectual elite of this country and that they should formulate plans to use that valuable commodity which so far has been going to waste. But there would be no use in asking them to do this kind of thing unless they could be assured that they could follow it up. They should therefore be assured of adequate finances to put into effect a plan of increased bursaries. I like the word ""bursaries"" rather than the word ""scholarships"". A person who himself, through the generosity of his own people, can afford to proceed to university should be allowed to do so. It is those who have not that opportunity whom I think this government and all governments should assist. If a plan could be formulated and approved by the government, then I think we would be doing something to fill a need in the industrial potential of this country.

Lastly, I want to return for a moment to what I said about technicians. I said, with some heat, perhaps, that we have one school. Through the forceful effort of the Ontario department of education and the persistence of its present principal and others they established a school to do a particular job, namely, the training of tradesmen, if you like, mechanics and technicians, who are found in that large industrial centre. They have done a splendid work, but it is not enough. When I think that it was my pleasure to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) lay the foundation stone of a post office in Vancouver that cost something over

$10 million or $15 million-and there are lots of them in the country-and we have one technical school worthy of its name, I just think that it is out of proportion. I know that the federal government is besieged with requests for all kinds of things. There are many desirable things that cost a lot of money that we cannot have, but I do feel that since we are growing in industrial stature we should do something drastic to man our industries.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Alexander Drew,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824588,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.3,1956-01-26,f2bbf383-7eb4-4502-a636-9fe5ed8129ea,ca.m.5171,Mr. R. R. Knight (Saskatoon):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate very heartily the mover of this private member's resolution. I am tempted to divert for a moment to express an opinion as to the value of private members' resolutions. I suppose this particular resolution about a subject which I think is vital may well do one or two things. It will air that important question before the country through the medium of this house. It will give us here an opportunity of discussing the matter and expounding our opinions in regard to it, and I think it will have some result in the creation of public opinion in favour of the particular proposition it advances.

This, of course, is not a new subject for myself; so much so, that I got tired of debating it, and did not think it was my duty to keep on. If the hon. member may be said to have in a way adopted a child that was at least partly my baby, I suppose that is all right because when one adopts some other person's baby he at least pays some tribute to the respectability of the family. This is not, of course, my particular cause; it is a cause that has been shared by many hon. members.

Before getting into the main debate, I should like to say I am interested to see my own people back at home taking an interest in this matter. I fancy the letter I hold in my hand, which was sent to me by the president of the student council of the University of Saskatchewan, or one something like it, has been received by many hon. members, because I am given to understand that a campaign is being put on by the students themselves to try to hasten the coming into effect of this resolution by way of legislation.

As I say, the letter was sent by the student council of the University of Saskatchewan. May I say briefly what they have in mind? They point out that many of the students in attendance at the university at the present time are in need of financial assistance; that many others who are not there have been prevented from attending owing to financial need. They point out that the cost of education generally has increased and is increasing

gadgets, faster cars, bigger refrigerators and die rest of it. I suggest that there may be something wrong with o-ur sense of value. Perhaps we are growing materialistic and acquisitive. In that we are aided and abetted continually by commercial advertising, and :he worst of it is that it tries to increase our lesire to surpass our neighbours in what are actually tinsel propositions. We are urged ;o buy what they call swanky cars and are cold that we will be able to look out of the sack windows and see our neighbour left sehind. What an inducement that is!

I am going to suggest that perhaps we should hasten slowly in these things. We should not be in a hurry to exploit all our natural resources, to get our hands upon all the money at once, and improve our standard of luxurious living. Perhaps we should plough back some of that capital investment, some proportion of our gross national product, and invest more of it in the creation of the good life. By good life I mean things tike health and education and those things which rightly or wrongly we are inclined to talk about as being the fine arts.

We have passed the pioneer stage. We have dug the stones and cut the stumps. We are very comfortably off, and it becomes a question of how we are spending our money. Are we squandering it or are we spending it on things which will build our country into a great nation?

I am reminded of a dear old friend of mine at home in the old country. Perhaps I should not refer to it in that way because my home has been here for 50 years or so and my children have been born here. But one does think of the land of his birth. I went back for a visit and was still a young man at that time. I went to see this dear aid friend as she sat in her little cottage in the green fields of Northern Ireland. It was only a thatched-roof cottage but it was dean, the walls were white and the roses were growing around the door. This little aid lady in the evening of her years was sitting there among her flowers, her pictures ind her books, particularly her books. Being mpetuous and young I began boasting about ;he good things we had in Canada, the indentions and other modern things. She sat and listened to me with patience and then she said, ""Yes son, perhaps you have a better standard of living, but perhaps we have a setter life."" It was something to think about. Perhaps she was quite wrong, but that is something that has lingered in my memory ""rom that day to this.
One of these items of the better life I lave been talking about is covered by the [DOT]esolution proposed by my hon. friend. He s suggesting more university scholarships.

We have to give these young people a chance if we are going to bring them up to be the kind of young people we want them to be, the kind of young people we need in our social and economic environment. A comprehensive scholarship plan involves increased accommodation. If the number of individual scholarships is increased it means increased attendance at the universities. I welcome that. These people will be running to our doors just as the people in Saskatchewan have been running to the doors of the hospitals under the hospital scheme. They need to run to those doors. God bless them, let them run, the more the better, so far as universities are concerned. I would not suggest that about hospitals.

This is going to impose a burden upon our universities and they can carry no more now because their burden is already too great. They are in a state of continuing and developing financial crisis. So assistance to universities paralleling grants to individuals will be needed. These things have been expressed much better than I can express them by university men of this country. The president of McGill University has been referred to today, also the late well-beloved Dr. R. C. Wallace of Queens, and also Dr. Sidney Smith who wrote a most interesting article in the University of Toronto Quarterly.

Someone has suggested that more should be done by business interests. I am not quite sure about that. I have not thought my way through to the end on that. To me education is a public responsibility and I do not want to rely on the profits of some candy firm or brewery or something else for the education of my children and my children's children. I think it is a public and therefore governmental responsibility. Nor do I want to be dependent upon distilleries to provide opportunity for my grandchildren's participation in sports or for awards that might come to them in that respect.

That reminds me that we already receive some foreign aid for education in this country, and I am referring now to what are known as foundations. I like to see money being given for education, but the people who run these foundations are beginning to think that this country is not carrying out its share of responsibility in regard to education. I am not able to quote this as a fact, but I have heard and read that some of these people are threatening to withdraw their support because the public of this country apparently do not sufficiently appreciate the gifts that are being made at least not sufficiently to match the outside assistance. Perhaps some of my hon. friends will be able to state whether that statement is true or not. I see some affirmative nods.

Our young people are clamouring for admittance to the halls of learning. I understand that between 7 and 8 per cent are now in attendance, but this percentage will increase, certainly under the scheme we are proposing today. The actual numbers will increase in any event. I think Dr. Smith estimated a total of 130,000 will be in attendance at the universities in ten years, or he may have been quoting an estimate by the bureau of statistics.

The logical question is, what does the government propose when faced with that particular situation? Is this proposed investment worth while or is it not? Is this the best way in which we can spend our money or is it not? Are we going to keep on putting our capital investment towards the manufacture of more gadgets and increasing our present luxurious state of living? It is quite true that luxury is enjoyed by everybody, and we would like to see it more generally shared, perhaps. But are we also going to look toward the future needs of this nation?

I think it is fair to say that the government has shied away from certain propositions in regard to education, certainly one that I have often advocated. What have they done about UNESCO? Have we as a country assumed our responsibilities? Have we from the early beginnings developed something worth while? We just shied away from it. In this connection I should like to quote the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I do not know whether he realises it or not, but one of his favourite expressions is ""at this time"": at this time we are not prepared to do anything. But that statement does hold out some hope for the future and hope is always a good thing. I am suggesting that we have shied away from these things, perhaps unnecessarily.

I think it is time that Canada grew up educationally. It is true that we have got rid of some of our inferiority complexes and are beginning to develop some of our native arts and literature, but we should be developing something for our children to read. When you give your child or grandchild 25 cents or 35 cents to go out and buy something to read, what does he come back with? What is available to him at that price. I say no more. Of all the countries I have ever been in there is in this country the greatest dearth of good reading for children.

The comparison simply leaves us astonished and ashamed. As far as my observation goes in this matter of a demand for education and for equality of opportunity in education, the government should be taking the lead in promoting higher learning by assisting those provinces which administer the systems of

education. We should have a scheme of national university scholarships and we should have it now. I am glad to hear members on the Liberal side advocating it. When one of the gentlemen on the other side advocates some progressive measure such as this, we begin to think that they are getting some encouragement or that at least no prohibition is being placed on them against mentioning the nasty word ""education"" in this sacred house devoted to federal matters.

To go back to the scheme of my hon. friend, this scheme would be of inestimable value to the young people of this country, to the provinces of this country and to the nation as a whole. The welfare of the nation as a whole, as well as that of the provinces and the municipalities, is, in my opinion, directly dependent on the quality of the education of its citizens. Canada did something more than help many returned soldiers when it instigated the D.V.A. education grants. She contributed to the efficiency of the whole nation. Let us not forget that the scheme was operated with individuals who on the average would certainly not have attained the same standard of education as the people to whom we are proposing that these bursaries or scholarships should now be given. If we made a success of that, if we made our country better or stronger because of that plan, what are we now waiting for? Not money
I have dealt with that. We have money for other things.

I say I am glad that a member who supports the government brought in the resolution. I honour him for it and I wish him luck with it. It may be a good sign. Let us hope it is of some significance. Let us hope that something will be done.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Robert Ross (Roy) Knight,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f2bbf383-7eb4-4502-a636-9fe5ed8129ea&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824589,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.4,1956-01-26,29120c21-7fca-48fe-bd93-53ba86e83429,ca.m.5071,Mr. A. J. MacEachen (Inverness-Richmond):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) on his interest in the education of the young people of Canada as exemplified in the resolution now under discussion. This resolution calls for consideration of the need to provide national scholarships and bursaries for university students in financial need. In supporting this resolution, I am responding to an invitation from the students of St. Francis Xavier University, who were kind enough to forward me a resolution outlining their views on this problem of such importance to the university population.
Until my election to the House of Commons,
I spent all of my adult life in university, either as a student or as a teacher, and it is upon that experience I wish to draw in giving voice briefly to my views on this subject.

In drawing attention to the need of financial assistance for university students, the hon. member for York Centre has singled out one of several problems involved in the task of making Canadian universities more effective instruments in the progress of Canada and in the intellectual and moral formation of its people.

Equally important is the question of direct financial assistance to the universities and expanded aid to programs of research, especially in the field of the social and economic sciences. This resolution, however, is not intended to provide a basis for the analysis of the total financial problem of the university and is therefore confined to the aspect of providing greater opportunities to the youth of Canada for securing a university education.

I do not share the attitude which regards a university education as solely useful in rising to a higher income status'or as replenishing the groups in the community who have exercised, in a traditional sense, social and cultural power. University education in a growing country must always have in mind the equipping of persons with skills for useful public service. It must be directed to the object of reducing social and geographical differences and divisions through its availability to all groups in a community. Finally, it must assist citizens to reach understanding by allowing them to share in the intellectual and spiritual heritage which it is the universities' duty to transmit.

I believe it is proper that each person should be allowed to choose freely his occupation. If the selected occupation requires university training, then a life ambition should not be thwarted and a contribution to society lost because the aspiring student has not the financial means. It may be that as society evolves, the notion of a university education will not be so closely bound with a gainful occupation but will be cherished as a desirable possession in its contribution to personal enrichment; and fortunate indeed is the community in which such persons abound.

If the case for assistance to university students is sound or appealing on theoretical grounds, it is more than justified by the needs of the present stage of Canada's development and is supported by the experience already gained in the launching of such assistance programs on a national scale.

Such favourable views exist on the success and efficacy of the education program of veterans under the D.VA. plan that it is really unnecessary to provide further proof. Let me say, however, that I had the opportunity of associating with veterans at one of our Canadian universities during the postwar years. These veterans were supported

in their university education by government funds and they were in part composed of students who would not have had a chance to pursue their education otherwise. This group made up a serious and competent element in the campus community. They were, of course, more mature than the average student group, but not the least of the reasons for their success as students was the removal of a great part of their financial concern. Today we have a program by which financial support is offered students who will enter the services upon graduation. Both these systems of aid are more than noble experiments. They are useful precedents. Their success nourishes the hope that, as the state supports university students in reward, and to provide an inducement, for service in the armed forces, it will also make generous provision for students who are ready to serve in peaceful pursuits.

I do not intend to retrace the ground covered by other speakers who have stressed the demand for trained persons in many professions in our present expanding economy; of the need to provide assistance in Canada to university students on a basis at least comparable to that provided in the United States and the United Kingdom; of the need to supplement the summer earnings of students through the provision of financial assistance; of the desire to increase the proportion of our population in university or with university experience.

These arguments appeal to Canadians who wish to pursue the development of their country and Canada's capacity to make a wider contribution in the cause of peace. The Canadian public will support the purpose of this debate. In the province of Nova Scotia there still lives with undiminished strength a love for learning and I am sure that a similar feeling exists in all other parts of Canada.

I want to touch for a moment on the view sometimes expressed that paying one's way sifts out those students who really want university education and who will really benefit from it. This process of paying one's way is regarded as a great builder of character. I prefer to think that a university builds character in a different sense, in the true sense of graduating men whose lives and conduct are patterned on immutable principles of religion and philosophy. But we are today also bent on building a country, and it is my belief that it will be built more solidly and more quickly if a greater share of people graduate from our universities.
The process of university education is not a financial process. It is rather a moral and intellectual process. Education extending into
the professional and graduate fields requires discipline and hard work that make it so essential to remove at least in part the financial worries.

I have said nothing, Mr. Speaker, about the amount of such assistance, what standards of scholarship should be set as qualification, or how it could be administered. These are decisions that may provoke a type of discussion which at this time might frustrate the purpose of the resolution, namely, to establish the need for assistance to university students as a compelling national concern.

,Liberal,,Allan Joseph MacEachen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=29120c21-7fca-48fe-bd93-53ba86e83429&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824590,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.5,1956-01-26,9adbd346-30dd-4c27-b96d-ca09f2e4158c,ca.m.2495,Mr. J. A. Smith (Battle River-Camrose):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate the mover of the resolution. It is my opinion that in presenting this resolution to the house he has brought before the members a problem that needs to be given great concern. As a former teacher, I should also like to pay tribute at this time to the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) for his efforts throughout the years in trying to secure federal aid for education. For many years the hon. member for Saskatoon has seen fit to place resolutions on the order paper requesting aid for education. He is well known throughout western Canada as a champion of aid for education.

We in this group intend to support the resolution primarily because we believe that the advantages derived from university training should be made available to all young men and women who would like to take advantage of such training. We do not feel that the young person who lacks the financial means to attend university should be deprived of that privilege. Again, Mr. Speaker, as a group we believe that the acceptance of the resolution would be good, sound business on the part of all hon. members.

If it can be said that any good at all comes out of war, perhaps the policy of giving aid to the young men and women who were fortunate enough to return to their native land as veterans of world war II and the Korean war would be at the top of the list. The young men and women who availed themselves at that time of this opportunity are now serving their country more effectively and are proving themselves to be of great value to their communities. Without going too far back in history, it is possible to find instances where other nations have recognized the value of education, particularly university training. I am thinking in terms now of the Japanese empire. Within the span of a few short years Japan was able to build itself into a power that threatened our western civilization. How did she do that? She selected the very best of the Japanese young people. Where were they sent? They
were sent to such countries as Great Britain, the United States, Germany and France. For what purpose? To pick up ideas and bring them back to Japan in order to make that nation powerful and strong.

I should also like to point out that Hitler in his early days took over control of the schools and universities of his country and that with this control he was able to build up in Germany that terrible war machine which threatened us for years. What is Russia doing today? In the course of the debate it has already been pointed out that as far as the communist government of Russia is concerned university training is a must. On the other hand, what are we doing? Are we looking to the future? Are we saying to our young people: We want you to go to the universities of our land?

In this country we have some of the finest universities to be found in the world. Are we saying to our young people: We want you to go there and equip yourselves so that you can take your place in our democracy and assist us in the cold war now being waged? Surely, Mr. Speaker, it must be recognized that we need something other than guns, bombers and so on to counteract the evil forces surrounding us today. We need educated young men and women who are firmly conviced that our way of life is the true and only way of life.

As a former teacher I have all too often watched young boys and girls come up through the school system and graduate from grade 12 with good marks only to go no further with their training. Why? It was not because they did not want to do so but because they did not have the financial means to carry on. In my opinion this is a sad situation. Education should and must be made available to all young people throughout Canada who desire and are capable of taking it. We are very pleased to support the resolution.

,Social Credit,,James Alexander Smith,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=9adbd346-30dd-4c27-b96d-ca09f2e4158c&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824591,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.6,1956-01-26,e150e6ec-4859-4cdf-b757-b176735adb61,ca.m.9127,Mr. S. R. Balcom (Halifax):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, I was asked some time ago by the students of Dalhousie University to support the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) when he presented his resolution, and I am very pleased to do so. A good case has been made for the desirability of more scholarships for university students by hon. members who have already spoken. Coming from a province where the need is great, may I say that we find there is a wide gap between what students can earn in their holiday periods and the cost of a year at university. The figures quoted by the national federation of Canadian university students show average earnings of $600 for men and $300 for

women compared with an outlay of somewhere around $1,200. The figure of $1,200 for a year may be conservative. The difference has to be made up in some way. The result is that the decision whether or not to go to university hinges very often on the immediate financial circumstances of a student's family.

If the parents are able to take care of the cost of higher education it is all to the good. If not, the student who gets his or her training the hard way does so with considerable sacrifice and hardship. This in itself is not a bad thing, provided it does not interfere with a proper use of their time at college and thus prevent them from getting a well-rounded education.

A survey in 1950 showed that over half of those who drop out of school or college do so for financial reasons. But there are those who, willing though they be to make the necessary sacrifices, are still not able to go further than high school. This seems to be the breaking point for many students. In order to confirm this view, one has only to look at the number of college students in Canada in comparison with the total population in the college-age group. In 1952 four per cent of those between the ages of 15 and 24 were attending university in Canada.

Attention has been drawn to the position in Canada as compared with that in other countries. In the United Kingdom and in France a large proportion of the students receive government scholarships and assistance. In Canada only about 15 per cent of our student population-whether the figure is correct or not I do not know-is assisted through scholarships and bursaries. These are not government scholarships, for the most part.

Hardly anyone would quarrel with the objective of the national federation of Canadian university students in asking for a national scholarship program. When a potential student is turned away from our colleges or professional schools not because of lack of ability but because he or she cannot afford to attend, we are all losers. The individual himself loses the opportunity for his broadest development and our society is that much the poorer. I am thinking not only in terms of technical training but in terms of those other qualities of breadth of vision and tolerance which are just as essential to our way of life.

The experience of Canadian universities with student veterans under the D.VA. scheme clearly showed that there is represented in the youth of Canada a great deal of ability that ordinarily does not have the

opportunity to make its full contribution to the development of this country. Because of economic difficulties many gifted young people are unable to attend university even though they have the necessary talent to become doctors, teachers, clergymen, scientists or engineers. Although they have the ability necessary to give outstanding service to Canada they are deprived of the opportunity to contribute their full potential because of the lack of university education.

Reports from universities throughout Canada have shown that the record of the student veterans was exceptionally good and that it in fact helped to set a new standard. This record was partly due to the fact that the student veterans were somewhat more mature than their classmates but it stands also as a clear reminder that we are not taking full advantage of the potential we have.

Canada is still a young and expanding country. If it is to make the progress which all true Canadians hope for, it must make the maximum use of its most valuable asset, namely the ability and skill of its youth.

Today industries and businesses all over the country are literally clamouring for men with university education to fill positions in the technical fields and in management. The same thing is true of government services. Dozens of recruiting teams are visiting the universities in search of such talent and many times they are obliged to go away with empty hands.

The universities of my own province of Nova Scotia have a special interest in this problem for two reasons. First of all, Nova Scotia has been traditionally the source of a disproportionately large number of professional men and of leaders in business and finance. Second, the average income in Nova Scotia is only about half that in Ontario. It is therefore correspondingly more difficult for our young people to find the money required to fulfil their ambition for a university education. At this point I might say that in Nova Scotia we have more students per capita than has any other province in Canada.

However, I am not sure that a national scholarship scheme is the first step that should be taken. Certainly such a program launched by itself to increase the student body substantially at this time, by whatever means, would impose on some of our colleges an impossible burden; for, in most cases, the tuition fees of the students cover only a portion of the cost of their courses. This is especially true of the medical and dental faculties where roughly only one-quarter of the costs are

covered by their fees. However, there is a substantial difference in all faculties. An influx of new students, whatever the source of their tuition, would only increase the demand for services already overtaxed.
