1824593,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.8,1956-01-26,e150e6ec-4859-4cdf-b757-b176735adb61,ca.m.9127,Mr. Balcom:,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,"Mr. Speaker, to continue the discussion of national scholarships where we left off at six o'clock, already during this session I have emphasized the need for a more generous policy of assistance by the federal government to our universities. Further financial aid is needed to enable the universities to make proper provision for salaries, for library research facilities and for all the other demands of modern education. We must emphasize quality and standards at this level. The institutions must have the best to offer or the students will turn away with dust and ashes instead of with capacities developed and attitudes that are healthy for responsible citizens.

Incidentally, I reiterate what I have said many times in this house namely, that the present method of distributing federal grants for education, resulting in a per capita rate per student so much lower than in most other provinces and so much less than that granted to provinces whose universities, being state supported, receive large benefits from the public purse, is a continuing source of dissatisfaction to the people whom I am proud to represent.

I am not suggesting that the government should bear the whole burden of cost. The Lord forbid that it should ever happen in Canada that the government should contribute so much money that they might possibly think that they should step in and have something to say in the operation of the universities. Individual graduates, business and industry, professional organizations and labour unions all have a stake and should make a voluntary contribution.

In no case that I know of do students' fees cover the cost of training. A graduate should take some responsibility for the continuance, the growth and improvement of the institution to which he owes a great deal. This sense of loyalty and responsibility is very important, not only in this connection, but throughout our whole society.
Under this resolution we are discussing and recommending scholarships and bursaries, but I believe the brief of the students should

be broadened so as to make loans to students one of its main objectives. I believe the bright, ambitious students coming out of high school need loans which, with their summer work, would carry them through their full course, these loans to be eventually paid back; for today we realize that graduates in medicine, engineering, geology and other faculties have no difficulty in making a repayment.

I would be inclined to broaden the intent of this resolution with the suggestion, too, that hospital schools for nurses' training, provided that they meet the requirements of the various nursing associations' regulations, be included. We have a youth training program which was mentioned today, and which last year expended over $514,000 in Canada, of which only $46,000 went to Nova Scotia.

Then, in 1954 I think it was, the Department of Veterans Affairs, in its progressive legislation, brought in the education assistance act, under which the sons and daughters of deceased veterans are enabled to receive an educational course extending over four years. During that time their tuition fees are paid and they also receive an allowance of $25 a month. This assistance extends over the whole four years. I note from the booklet issued by the Department of Veterans Affairs that this course is extended to approved teaching hospitals which lead to registered nurses' degrees.

Then again we have one of the programs that were instituted by the Department of National Defence. I am not certain of the army and air force, but I know of the Royal Canadian Navy. Under this program university students join the reserve force and go into training. Over a period of their college course they receive something like $185 a month while they are on active service during the summer months, and during the study period in the winter months they receive half that amount. That seems to me to be very generous, and it has been taken advantage of by students all over Canada. In addition to all these benefits, a great many of these men go on tours and receive training in other points of interest all over the world.

The federal authority also contributes to the building and operation of provincial vocational schools. Any financial help that would educate and broaden our Canadian citizens should be assisted. I have in mind scholarships and bursaries to encourage all Canadians to learn the French and English languages. Let us do more to develop our bilingualism and consider it fitting, as obviously some help is needed, to do everything possible to make our two languages truly national.
By all means I would support this resolution and I would add that the government should consider the advisability of further aid to universities generally.

,Liberal,,Samuel Rosborough Balcom,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e150e6ec-4859-4cdf-b757-b176735adb61&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824594,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.9,1956-01-26,ea30e79d-1feb-461a-bbea-b3e5a570ee30,ca.m.468,Mr. G. C. Nowlan (Digby-Annapolis-Kings):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, this is one of the important matters which I think confront the country today. It is a very complex problem and one on which one could speak at considerable length if one had the opportunity so to do. But I do know that many hon. members wish to discuss this matter tonight, and I propose to speak very briefly indeed.

In the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the other day I referred to the problem of university education, but I am not going to develop that further tonight. It is an anomalous situation in which we find ourselves in this country today, and which this resolution actually envisages. Practically every university in Canada is being taxed to the limit today to provide accommodation and service for the student body that is attending those universities at the present time. This resolution envisages the fact that still more students will be attending the universities. I think that is true, but it certainly does emphasize the fact that it is a complicated problem and not a simple one. The time has come when the government of Canada, the people of Canada generally, in co-operation with and through the provinces as well, will have to give more attention to the university's problem than has been given heretofore.

We have had many interesting debates on the matter contained in the resolution which is now before us. The atmosphere has been fairly well cleared with respect to it. Very little action has been taken. As I said, the time is rapidly approaching when some concrete action must be taken.

As I pointed out the other day, we are expecting an increase in our population. We look to world leadership, and we speak about the heritage which is ours and the challenge which is ours. The business leaders throughout this country are all saying we have to produce much more leadership material than is being produced at the moment. That must be done to a substantial extent through the universities. I realize it is only one phase of an over-all educational system. It is the one which is perhaps the most important and the most critical.
This resolution deals with only one phase of the problem, namely, the scholarship problem and the matter of financial support to students, and it is on that that I am going to speak for a moment.
Perhaps I can speak with a little feeling on this subject, coming as I do from a small

university town where I have lived all my life. I have watched boys and girls come there seeking employment and seeking to put themselves through university. I know what small scholarships or bursaries mean to these people. I was thrilled to read the other day in the Globe and Mail-and the statement also appeared in newspapers all across Canada-that a contribution had been made to medical science by a research man in a certain Canadian university. I shall not mention his name. I happen to remember that fellow when he came to Acadia 20 years ago. I know that through a little influence he was able to obtain a job as a waiter in the university dining hall and thereby put himself through college. When I read of his contribution in the paper the other day I thought to myself, that is a substantial contribution that is being made to the public welfare of this country and to the world arising from the fact that this fellow happened to be able to get a job.

I have known, as has, I am sure, every hon. member in this house, scores and hundreds of young people who have not been able to obtain jobs at all. Some have been able to work and put themselves through, some have had relatives who sacrificed and put them through, some have won scholarships, but some have had to fall by the wayside. This resolution, as I see it, envisages this responsibility and suggests that something more must be done to assist the Canadian students who want to make a real contribution to their country if they are given an opportunity to do so.

In giving assistance to the veterans we have not established a pattern but we have established a precedent which was a notable one carried out by this government or by this parliament-I do not care how you put it. In doing so we have made a great contribution to this country, one from which we are only now beginning to reap the benefits. National research scholarships are of tremendous importance and I know that the Minister of National Defence and his department have provided for the education of many young men and possibly of some young women provided they will undertake to enter the armed forces and stay there for a certain length of time. To date, however, our contributions have been haphazard and I feel that the time has come when we should try to put them into better focus. I am not complaining about what we have done in this direction but I would suggest that it has been inadequate. I say this because the national research scholarships and others in large part deal with graduate students. We must not overlook the fact that we also have the problem of the undergraduate student

According to figures released by the bureau of statistics we are able to estimate that by 1960 the secondary school population of this country will have doubled, a 100 per cent increase over 1950. In a few years' time the students represented by that 100 per cent increase will be moving on towards university. Many of them need assistance in order to reach that goal. Universities also need assistance in increasing their facilities for dealing with the students. As I say, there is the undergraduate problem as well as the graduate problem.

My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Fairey) in speaking this afternoon mentioned the need for further technical study in Canada. I realize that this is important but I do not think our country is going to develop solely along material lines. I think the emphasis on the sciences and on technical studies can be overdone. You, sir, will remember that in the old days in your province the emphasis was on the classical studies, generally speaking. I think there should also be an emphasis on the humanities or social sciences. History, economics, et cetera, must not be overlooked in the days that lie ahead, as they might very easily be. There are no scholarships for studies such as these and generally speaking there are no scholarships for graduate students. For these reasons I welcome this resolution. I think it is bringing the problem- and I think it is a national problem-into focus. I must emphasize again, however, that it is only one phase of the problem because the problem of education is much more complex than this. However, I think the time has come when the nation as a whole must assume responsibility for this matter and must set up a system perhaps privately supported in part, or supported by the provinces in part and supported only in part by the dominion of Canada as a nation.

I hope we can inaugurate national scholarships whereby young men such as the one I mentioned a few moments ago and the thousands like him who will be coming along will be given the opportunity of obtaining a college education and will thus be able to make a contribution to this country and to the world.
Mr. Speaker, I heartily support the resolution.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Clyde Nowlan,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ea30e79d-1feb-461a-bbea-b3e5a570ee30&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824595,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.10,1956-01-26,273960a5-f067-4902-953e-30912d31347f,ca.m.8204,Mr. Daniel Mclvor (Fort William):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, I will be brief as usual. Many teachers have asked me at this time to support a resolution of this kind and although I shall support the resolution I have certain ideas of my own on the subject of education which I should like to express.

I think that if a young man-or woman- has a purpose in life he will eke his way through college. Canadian students do not want a handout from anyone-not even from the government of Canada-because if they have a strong purpose in life they will find a way to graduate from college. I could name men in this house, including the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Fairey) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who worked their own way through college because they had a purpose in life. We do not want to graduate a lot of sissies. If a man has a purpose in life he will achieve what he sets out to do and will serve God and his country and there will be no strings attached to it. If a student receives aid from the government of Canada or from any province he should, after he has graduated and is earning his living in law or some other field, be man enough to pay back the taxpayers' money. I realize that those who were overseas are in a different position and those veterans who have graduated from college are a credit to Canada. I could name a good many of them, including some who came from the city of Fort William.
I think this resolution deserves consideration but we do not want to jump on the band wagon simply because it is a popular attitude.

Mr. J. W. Nose worthy (York South): Mr. Speaker, it is very encouraging indeed to many of us to find the Liberals vying with the opposition in an effort to get the floor in order to speak on the subject now before us. It is extremely interesting and also gratifying to find this resolution coming from the Liberal benches.

The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), who has just taken his seat, for whom everybody in the house has a great deal of respect, has made the point that students today are not seeking government aid. He seemed to imply that in his day and in mine students were made of sterner stuff and were able to earn their own way through university. I was unfortunate enough to be one of those who had to earn their own way in order to go to university at all. When I attended the University of Toronto my freshman year, 1912, cost me less than $200. My room, board and university fees together amounted to $150. Some of us have attended, or have had our children attending, university in more recent years and we realize that what kept me at university for a year would not today keep a young person for a month at a university. It is true that it is possible for young people to earn more during their summer vacations than it was in my time, but the spread between the cost

and what can be earned is much greater now than it was years ago. Most of us know from experience that today it is practically impossible for young people to work their own way through university and pay all their expenses.

One cannot help noting the interest in education which is shown in this chamber today as compared with the attitude when I came to the house in 1942. At that time we considered education so exclusively a provincial matter that we scarcely dared mention the word in this chamber. During my first session here I was ruled out of order on three different occasions when I attempted to bring before the house a subject matter similar to that which we are discussing today.

Debates on education have been welcomed in this chamber now for some years and in every party in the house we find supporters for some form of federal government assistance. I have often maintained here that, notwithstanding the British North America Act, education is a matter of great concern to Canada as a nation. No provincial department of education educates a child to become a citizen of that province alone. Those who are educated in the province of Quebec move into every other province of Canada, and many of those who are educated in Ontario do likewise. Whether the cost of education is borne by the municipality, by the provincial government or with assistance from the federal government, we are educating young people today as Canadian citizens and not as citizens of any one province.

The level of culture and education to which we can bring our young people, regardless of the province in which they live, is a matter of interest and concern to Canada as a whole. We recognize that fact in time of war when we spend federal money in order to educate men and women to play their part in the war effort in order to equip them to be better soldiers, sailors, airmen and workers in munitions factories. There was no quarrel with the provincial governments over the expenditure of federal money for education in time of war. Why should we consider war so much more important in the life of the nation than peace, or education in time of war so much more important than education for peaceful living?

We are inclined to measure our progress today in terms of economics. We are hearing constantly of the great development of our natural resources and the ever-expanding production of our factories. We estimate our total national product solely in material terms. We forget that there are other values in life than those material things which can be estimated in dollars and cents.

A very learned economist, Dr. Galbraith, a Canadian who is now professor of economics at Harvard University, appeared before the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects a few days ago and he had this to say regarding the value we set on progress:

More urgent than resource development is the problem of human development, and Canada, like the United States, has suffered an enormous wastage of talent by making higher education dependent not on ability, but on ability to pay.

I do not think there is anyone in this chamber who does not recognize the truthfulness of that statement. Today our universities are crowded but the people who are selected or who find it possible to attend are not necessarily the young people with the greatest ability or those who can profit best by a university education. By and large they are those who have the ability to pay for a university education. Dr. Galbraith made another significant statement when he said:

But far more Important than resource development Is the problem of human development. The most serious current failure In both Canada and the United States Is the failure to keep abreast of the technical and scientific requirements of growth.
The present scramble for highly qualified people is a measure of our failure. We must plan to spend generously to correct our mistakes in this area.

If Canadians are to keep abreast of the times, if Canadian industry is to be supplied with specialists who are Canadians, then we must find the means of permitting many of our ablest young people who cannot now attend university to be able to do so. Even at that, we have fallen behind in providing specialists in the fields of natural science and engineering. But we have fallen much farther behind the times in the provision of graduates in the humanities, the arts and the social sciences. If we are to make this nation the best nation possible, if we are to produce a race of Canadians who can hold their own with the peoples of other countries, then we must be prepared to spend more money and to give more attention to those things which cannot be measured in terms of dollars and cents, those things which will eventually add to human happiness and development.

This is a matter which today has very broad support throughout the country. Even as conservative a group as the Canadian chamber of commerce in its December newsletter commented on the fact that we in Canada are not training our young people of the greatest ability for the positions they will be needed to fill.

This afternoon we heard that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), who have returned from their trips behind the iron curtain, were greatly impressed by

the urge to learn in those countries and by the opportunities for learning provided there. True, we may think that much of what is learnt there may be communist doctrine. We may not approve of the tactics that are used. But we dare not ignore the fact that behind the iron curtain the communists are providing for their young people every possible opportunity to gain an education, such as it is.

If we are to maintain our position in the battle for men's minds that is now going on throughout the world, then it behooves us to see that provision is made whereby more of our most capable young people will be provided with an opportunity of attending university. I sincerely hope that some way can be found, within the limitations of the British North America Act and without overriding provincial authorities, to make those opportunities available from federal funds.

,Liberal,,Daniel (Dan) McIvor,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=273960a5-f067-4902-953e-30912d31347f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824596,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.11,1956-01-26,fa35eab4-2838-4cc0-a8fb-67604ad16c62,ca.m.6697,Mr. C. W. Carter (Burin-Burgeo):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, as one whose attendance at a university would have been impossible without the assistance provided by scholarships and bursaries, it gives me very great pleasure to support this resolution.

So much has already been said by previous speakers that the subject has now been rather well covered, but I believe the organization whose scholarships made it possible for me to attain a college education would have every reason to consider me lacking in appreciation and gratitude did I not take advantage of this opportunity to support this resolution.

In the light of the opening remarks by the hon. member for York South perhaps I should explain also that, in addition to the scholarships and bursaries, it was necessary for me to earn upward of $1,000 during my college term, and the financial worry and physical effort which that involved was a very serious handicap all through my college life. I therefore commend the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) for bringing this resolution before us today. In so doing, he has performed a service to our country by focussing our attention on a matter of vital national importance.

Canada is a country that is blessed with fabulous natural resources, and we are rightly concerned with their conservation and development. How much more, therefore, should we be concerned with the development of our human resources, which are the most important and most precious resources of all?

We hear a good deal about the wonders of the electronic brain. How much more wonderful is the human intellect, which has produced not only the electronic brain and automation but all the other wonders of 67509-38i

science which have contributed so much to our material comforts and conveniences. Up till now, every minute of man's life has been occupied in trying to survive. It is only now, with the perfection of the machine and the coming of the machine age, that man is beginning to find time to live. The very vastness of Canada's natural resources makes it all the more imperative that we develop our human resources, because the efficiency with which these natural resources are conserved for future generations, or developed and distributed among the living generations, will depend directly upon the development of our human resources.

The emphasis that Soviet Russia is placing upon education generally and upon university education in particular shows that they are very much aware of this fact. As the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) pointed out this afternoon, the Russian output of scientists and engineers will soon exceed that of all the countries of the free world combined. The very shortage of scientists, engineers, physicists, chemists, doctors, teachers and those of other professions in Canada shows that either we are not alive to the problem or that existing facilities are not adequate. In any case we are not meeting the need.

I was very glad to hear the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) emphasize the importance of the humanities. One of the causes of the troubles in the world today is that scientific training has far outstripped our moral and mental training. Material progress has outstripped our spiritual progress. Our greatest problems today are not scientific or economic. They are social and political. We need minds trained in the humanities to come to grips with these problems and find a way out. We need minds trained in science and the humanities to grapple with what is perhaps the greatest problem of our age-to find a way so that the wealth produced by the machine can be distributed, so that the machine can be employed with maximum benefit and all the blessings that can flow from the machine may be fully enjoyed by all mankind.

Another reason why I support the resolution is that it will help in some degree to offset one of the defects in our present system of education. Today our educational system is such that we try to educate our children en masse and because we do that the only selection of students that is made is that performed by the universities themselves. It sometimes happens that a person attends university who perhaps should not be there. He is there because his parents have money and ambition, and because they have money and ambition they decide that their son must

be a doctor, lawyer or engineer. Although he turns out to be only a very average student, because his parents have the means he is able to take one or even two years longer than necessary to secure a degree. On the other hand, there are many brilliant students who would be a great credit to a university, who would render great service to their country and their fellow men but who cannot get the necessary training because of lack of means.

The hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Fairey) drew attention to the waste of intellect and ability that is a product of our present educational system. As an ex-teacher and one who spent a number of years supervising schools I can testify to the accuracy of his statement. Time after time I saw tremendous talent, a tremendous brain, buried in some little outport village, a young person whose parents were barely existing on a subsistence level and who perhaps had no hope whatever of even being able to go to high school. Time after time I saw children with great talent for art, sculpture or music who were without the opportunity or even the hope of being able to develop these God-given talents.

The mover of the resolution has not given us very much information as to the methods by which the resolution might be implemented. As it stands now, it calls for grants to be furnished by the government. I believe there are greater possibilities than those implied in the terms of the resolution. I have become intrigued with the idea that it might be possible to tie in such scholarships with the idea of a national memorial to veterans of both wars. In the course of his remarks the hon. member for York Centre stressed the idea that such scholarships would serve to build unity in our nation, and if we can kill two or three birds with one stone I think we should endeavour to do so. It has occurred to me that if a student in Newfoundland received a scholarship given in memory of some deceased veteran from Quebec what a bond of unity would result. What an opportunity there would be for better understanding! Two different families from two different provinces and with two different backgrounds would have a mutual or common interest in each other and an incentive to learn more and more about the family, the background and the life of the person who was being commemorated by that scholarship. I do not know whether or not that idea is feasible. It just occurred to me as I was listening to the speeches this afternoon. I mention it because I think it deserves some consideration.
Perhaps it would be better not to set up any arbitrary rules as to how these scholarships might be implemented. Perhaps it would be

wiser to set up a committee that might consider all the aspects of the situation and make recommendations. I heartily agree with my friend the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom) in what he said about providing scholarships for nurses and for students who wish to become bilingual in the two official languages of our nation. I should like to go even further than he has gone. I should like to see scholarships provided for people who have talent for art and painting, music, singing and literary pursuits. All of these things are needed in Canada. All of them will enrich our culture and our nation.

Before I close, Mr. Speaker, I should like to offer just one more idea. I think it would be a fine thing if we could also extend some national scholarships to students of other countries, particularly to students from Asia, India and Africa. In November, 1954, it was my privilege to attend the conference of UNESCO at Montevideo in South America. While there I had occasion to meet a number of students who were proud to tell me that they had been educated in Canada, having been enabled to come to Canada by means of a scholarship. It was, of course, a scholarship that was provided by the university which they attended. In the interests of mutual understanding and in an effort to show our interest in our friends in other countries who are clamouring for education but who do not have the facilities we have, and who are trying to build up their own country and their own economy, I think it would be a great thing if we had something like a Colombo plan in education. I am sure that money spent in this way would come back repaid a thousandfold.

,Liberal,,Chesley William Carter,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=fa35eab4-2838-4cc0-a8fb-67604ad16c62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824597,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.12,1956-01-26,d25060a9-6d52-4461-a569-fc17c9e6d009,ca.m.654,Mr. W. G. Dinsdale (Brandon-Souris):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, last December by request of President Eisenhower some 2,000 United States educators met in Washington to discuss a national emergency. That national emergency was the United States school system which, according to this group, was rocking dangerously on its foundations and also on its premises. We in Canada would not approach the problem of education from that dramatic standpoint. However, from the interest displayed in this debate today, it is obvious that we are becoming more and more concerned about the problem of education in Canada.

As I look at the resolution before the house, it seems to me to be a nice, middle-of-the-way course between two other educational problems that have been discussed from time to time in this chamber. In the first instance there is the perennial resolution put forward

by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight). It suggests that consideration might be given to general federal aid for education. On the other hand we have the resolution of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) who draws attention to the fact that our research facilities in this country are far from adequate and that some action should be taken by the federal government to increase our activity in that regard.

To come to the resolution recommending a more extensive use of scholarships and bursaries in order to deal with this growing problem, it seems to me that it gets around the difficulty with which this parliament is always confronted when we discuss federal aid for education. I refer to the constitutional problem involving the exclusive right of the provinces to deal with any matters relating to education. I am happy to support the resolution that we have before us this evening. I say that it is encouraging to note the increased interest displayed by hon. members on all sides of the house and from all parts of Canada. However, if we look outside this chamber, Mr. Speaker, I think we shall find that there is an even more intense and wider interest in the matter of education-particularly on the university level-in Canada today.

When the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences was meeting in the various parts of Canada no less than 143 briefs presented to that commission made a suggestion to the effect that some form of bursary assistance should be made available to our brighter young people. As you scan through the recommendations of that report you find that two basic principles emerge relating to this matter. First of all, a democratic educational system must ensure that capable students shall not be prevented by financial need from completing their education. That is the first' general theme that runs through all the recommendations that were presented to the royal commission. The second general theme is that Canada's future development depends upon an adequate supply of intelligent and well-trained research scientists and scholars.

To deal with the first general principle, Mr. Speaker, it is of course obvious that we are not making the most of our potential human resources on the university level. We are not ensuring that capable students shall have the opportunity to proceed to advanced education. Unfortunately, the main deterrent to the realization of this end is the economic and financial factor. That of course is not the only deterrent. We are still a young nation. Some parts of the country are still in the frontier period of development, and on the frontier

in the outlying areas of the country there are neither the traditions that would encourage our younger people to continue their education on the higher level nor the personal incentive. Therefore, in addition to the financial and economic factor, we must also keep in mind that there are other problems producing Canada's relatively poor record on the level of higher education.

However, this resolution deals mainly with the economic and financial factor. From a personal contact with the problem in one of the western provinces, I can say there is a close relationship between the amount of schooling a child receives and the economic status of the parents. That conclusion has been arrived at by statistical analyses. You find that by far the larger percentage of your students at the university level come from relatively more well-to-do families in Canada.

It is true, as several hon. members have mentioned in this discussion, there was a time in the earlier stages of development that anybody who so desired could receive a university education by means of working his-way through college, and a good many hon, members have already given testimony of their own experience in this regard. Unfortunately, today costs have risen to such an extent in our universities; board, room and the costs of books and so forth, have risen so excessively that it is almost impossible for a student to go through college, and particularly to take some professional training, unless he has some form of financial assistance, or unless his family happens to be in the higher income brackets. Therefore it seems obvious to me, Mr. Speaker, that we need to broaden quite extensively the scholarship and bursary basis behind our system of higher education.

If we were to take the time to examine the bursary situation already prevailing in Canada we would find it to be totally inadequate. Most universities make a very noble gesture in this regard. Some commercial firms, and private corporations have provided very generous scholarships, scholarships of sufficient size to make it possible for an exceptional student to carry right through to the end of his professional training. But if you examine the catalogue of any of our universities you will find that most of the bursaries and scholarships are in the $200, $300, $400 or $500 category, and that is far from adequate to meet the average costs of a year at university today, which amount to something like $1,200. When only a small part of that necessary money is available, it becomes more of a headache than an asset in helping the

student to pursue his chosen course. I know that at the college in our own city, which is a liberal arts and sciences college, we get very generous support from the local merchants who give memorial scholarships of various kinds, but again they are within the smaller limits that I have already mentioned.

I want to make this observation. At the level of graduate studies, Canada is in a much better position than she is at the level of undergraduate studies. One of the reasons for this relatively better position in the graduate studies is the generous encouragement that Canada's national research council gives to graduate students pursuing advanced work in the field of the physical sciences. Of course, the national research council is sponsored by the federal government.

The Department of National Health and Welfare has also given some encouragement to graduate students. I should like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that good as this is, it is rather looking at the problem from the wrong end. In order to get to graduate level, you must proceed through four or five years of strenuous and expensive undergraduate activity, with the result that many of those who would be qualified to proceed to the rarefied atmosphere of graduate studies and become the leading scientists and scholars in this country are prevented from ever embarking on that worthy goal because they are stymied at the level of university entrance.

We should also note that a good many of our graduate students working in Canada have their eyes on the United States rather than on Canada when they have finally finished their courses of studies. One of the reasons is that the United States has a much more comprehensive program for graduates. They are quite happy to invite and to induce our brighter Canadian students across the border by means of their very generous scholarships program. We are constantly reminded that migration across the border has been taking place at rather alarming proportions for many years in Canada and unfortunately among the migrants are many of Canada's brightest young people, who go south to seek higher learning and pursue the wider opportunities available there. Therefore, I think we can conclude, without enlarging on the subject further, by saying that we are hardly providing a sufficient financial inducement to make it possible for bright young Canadians to pursue a course of study.

What about this other matter of the adequate supply of intelligent and well-trained research scientists? I will agree with those who have suggested tonight that not everybody is capable of making the most of a university

education. I think that is implicit in the resolution here before us because the program of scholarships and bursaries operates to a certain extent as a screening procedure. It encourages only the brightest and the most capable young people. I include in that phrase ""most capable"" not only those with the highest intellectual capacity but also those with that more intangible quality of character and moral stamina. In the very nature of a bursary program there is a tendency to encourage those who are qualified from that broader perspective. In fact, the royal commission has laid down specific recommendations as to the type of scholarship program which might be sponsored by the government of Canada. For instance, it suggests that 100 annual scholarships of $1,000 each might be made available to students of outstanding ability; only 100 annual scholarships mind you. It suggests further that 250 scholarships of $500 might be available and 2,000 bursaries of $500 for diligent students on the basis of need. That is not a particularly broad or comprehensive program but if we were to actually look at the picture presented by the normal curve of the distribution of intelligence the number of people in any population grouping who possess the higher intelligence quotient making it possible for them to take the best advantage of advance training is a relatively small percentage, 15 or 20 per cent of the total population at most. The rare category among the human species, those of unusual brilliance who are potential geniuses represents only 5 per cent of the total population. The tragedy is that many of our students who are possessed of this high degree of intelligence are denied the opportunity of advanced training to prepare themselves to serve in the various fields that are waiting for people of exceptional talent, because of economic factors, because of isolation from centres of university training and because of lack of incentive. The scheme proposed by the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences and supported by many hon. members here today would, I am sure, go a long way to deal with the very urgent problem that is confronting Canada at this time.

,Progressive Conservative,,Walter Gilbert Dinsdale,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d25060a9-6d52-4461-a569-fc17c9e6d009&Language=E&Section=ALL

Goode (Burnaby-Richmond):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, I have listened most attentively to this debate which has been held on a very high level. Most of the hon. members who have taken part in the discussion have been those gentlemen who have received university education and they knew something about the subject which they were discussing. I have not had a university education. I wonder what contribution to this debate would be made by the hon. member from Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) if he were in his

seat tonight? Many of us remember his telling us of the time that he drove a milk wagon through the streets of Vancouver. He also did not have the opportunity of a university education. I think my hon. friend from Medicine Hat who had such a distinguished career with the government of Alberta could make a valuable contribution. He could speak of the people whom he knew who had had university education whereas he and I did not have such an opportunity. I think, therefore, it would be of value if someone who has not had a university education should rise and contribute to the dis-cussibn on this resolution.

I had to leave school at grade 7; I did not complete grade 7. At that time I was 12 years of age. I had to go to work because of sickness in my family and I kept my small family on my wages which amounted to $15 a month. I frequently wonder how much a university education would have done for me. I had not completed grade 7 and I was one-half of 1 per cent away from the Governor General's medal in Saskatchewan. Two people in the school I attended could have been awarded the Governor General's medal. I was one-half of 1 per cent away from receiving it and the young man who did receive it had a father who could afford a university education. That young man's name is now a household word in Canada. I do not know what the future might have held for me if I had had the same advantages. However, that is an example of what can be accomplished with higher learning when one has financial resources behind one as compared to not having sufficient money to obtain university training.

As I said, I wonder what my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway would have said in this debate if he was not busy in his office at the moment. I can well imagine what he would have said about the advantages of having an education in his own inimitable way in regard to his associates. I also wonder what my friend the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) would have said in this debate. Without a university education he has done a magnificent job in the labour field, as we all know. Whether a university education would have assisted him is a matter of question but there is no doubt in my mind that it would not have hampered him in his career.

I wonder about the value of education in relation to the problem of juvenile delinquency which confronts us. Some time ago I was fortunate enough to be the chairman of the school board in Burnaby, and because I held that position I suppose I know a little about what young people think. I remember

that one young boy who was attending Burnaby South high school wanted to become a chemical engineer. His father was killed in a traffic accident and six months later he left high school and took a job delivering groceries in a truck. That young man was a potential scientist. I wonder what his contribution to our society would have been if this government or all governments had joined together to assist this young man who had attained wonderful marks in high school. I know of another young man who was working as a truck driver. He wanted to become a physician. His parents were killed in a train wreck just outside of Saskatoon some years ago. I wonder what this country is missing by not having the contribution of a young man with that type of mentality.

We have listened to several splendid speeches concerning the problem of juvenile delinquency. I wonder about the relationship between juvenile delinquency and the frustration of young people who get themselves into trouble partly because they envy other young people whose parents' financial position enables them to attend high schools and universities. I wonder if that frustration has anything to do with the juvenile delinquency problem in Canada? Perhaps not, but I suggest we give it some thought; it is a thought on the level of a man who never went to university. Perhaps those people who went to university could judge it in a different way. I envy the hon. member from Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) because he seems to know exactly of what he speaks in this matter. He puts it so well. I appreciate the experience behind the remarks of the distinguished hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Fairey) when he spoke in the debate this afternoon. By ability alone he became the deputy minister of education in his province. These men speak from experience.

I do not know whether someone like me, getting up in a debate like this and asking the government to spend more money for the greatest asset we can have, is making any contribution, but I have made what little contribution I could. I believe that with this government's help and the help of other governments every young person in Canada should have the opportunity to have his own future in his own hands.

,Liberal,,Tom Goode,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a66de47c-bf96-4e4e-ab1b-c2984f84a217&Language=E&Section=ALL

Macdonnell (Greenwood):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, I am tempted by reason of the last speech to digress for a moment, because while we are talking about university education tonight, and while those of us who have been at university would like to think that we have not wasted our time, nevertheless I think we all recognize that education is

not confined to university people. It so happens that when I was in business I was associated closely with two men neither of whom had ever been near a university. They were two of the best educated men I have ever known. Incidentally one of them could use the English language better than 90 per cent of university graduates, for the very simple reason that he had been saturated with the King James version of the Bible which had given him a beautiful English style.

1824600,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.15,1956-01-26,35a61aaf-7c98-4099-aa37-d5384b719315,ca.m.7340,Mr. Murphy (Lambion West):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,He would not be a Presbyterian?

,Progressive Conservative,,Joseph Warner Murphy,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=35a61aaf-7c98-4099-aa37-d5384b719315&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824601,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.16,1956-01-26,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. Macdonnell:,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,He was not a Presbyterian, no, and that was one of his few defects. I think we all ought to be grateful for this debate. We ought to be grateful to the mover of this motion, and we ought not to forget those to my left who have brought this matter up year after year and who have also made a notable contribution today.

It is interesting to be told by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) that when he came to this house 14 years 'ago they just did not talk about education. We have moved since that time and it is no longer so exclusively provincial. Those of us who have been associated with universities have every reason to be grateful for the substantial assistance which we have had from the dominion. As has been recalled tonight, we are also most grateful for what has been done, particularly in the realm of the national research council and in connection with war veterans.

One of the things that has interested me today is to realize that apparently university graduates are much more appreciated than they used to be. There was a time when people did not flaunt too much the fact that they were university graduates. It was considered that you had better get into business and try to make your way and win confidence and then let people discover gradually that you were a university graduate. There was a feeling in those days that a university graduate was apt to be high-hat and superior.

I would infer from what has been said during this debate that those days are pretty well past. It is clear that the need is great and the problem is going to press hard. It is not only a problem of technicians, but happily it seems clear that those in business who have to make selections from young people are appreciating much more than they did years ago that a broader education, which has been in danger of being shoved into the corner, particularly in wartime when
we had to stress the technical side so much, should now take a more important place in our educational program.

It seems to me that there are two or three questions which arise with regard to these scholarships. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) pointed out that there had been a tendency to regard scholarships as being confined to graduates and he stressed the fact that these scholarships should go to undergraduates as well. I find myself in sympathy with the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) when he suggests that there should be a lot of selfhelp in these matters. I was made rather dizzy when the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) said he had earned $1,000 toward his university course. I never got within sight of $1,000; if I earned $100 during the summer I thought I was doing pretty well. I am assured by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings that he was also under the dire necessity of earning his way through university.

The universities are going to be faced with tremendous problems. I am reading now from the Toronto University Quarterly in which they make the calculation that in 10 years from now there will be from 110,000 to

column2: in Canadian universities as compared with the present total of 65,000. I read to the house the other day a formidable series of comments by the British press reflecting the great burden which is being put on us in the matter of competition with Russian education.

column1: A suggestion has been made that a royal commission should be appointed. One is inclined to be afraid of royal commissions, but on the other hand it does seem to me that here is a problem every bit as important as the economic problem which is being studied by a royal commission. Indeed you could argue that to try to look forward into the course of our education is more important because if we do not have education, no matter what the royal commission may find as to our future, we will not be able to satisfactorily carry it out.

It seems clear to me after listening to the discussion that there are two sanctions, so to speak, for these scholarships. One is what you might term a scholarship given on an economic basis, by reason of need, and the other is a scholarship given on the basis of talent. That seems to me to involve very difficult questions. All universities are seeking scholarships which are usually scholarships for talent-I think I can say that almost universally they are scholarships for talent.

Of course the universities would be glad to get any assistance they can from governments. The Massey report made many recommendations as to scholarships, only a few of which I believe have been carried out. As I understand it, they are on the talent basis, what you would call the professional basis. They are to be given as assistance to all kinds of people whose talents we desire to cultivate and nurture.

It seems to me that the problem is a difficult one and I am wondering whether there is not some way in which the government and the university authorities could consult with each other. I am sure that the university authorities are constantly giving their best attention to this. I believe there is an association of university presidents. Even a believer in private initiative like myself would hope that in some way there could be a common plan, there could be co-operation among the universities and we would not be left just with the rugged individualism of each university doing what it could. I would hope that in some way there would be a plan.

It seems to me that the one thing that arises immediately is how far are we going to allow the problem which is being so much discussed, the tremendous technical progress of Russia, to twist or even to distort our education. How far are we going to maintain the balance between the humanities and technical subjects? I do not think I need take up the time of the house any longer. I feel that this is just as important as the economy of Canada, and somehow or other as a result of this discussion I would hope that progress could be made to this end.

Before I resume my seat I should like to say that I would not want university presidents to be faced suddenly with some cut and dried plan. I should think that the university presidents would be the best people to offer information as to how the matter might be studied, how progress might be made, because there are many aspects of this and it will require all the wisdom we can summon to solve them satisfactorily.

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL

1824604,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.19,1956-01-26,86cdb90c-8049-4642-8b59-ba1d2f99d892,ca.m.4312,Mr. J. A. Blanchette (Compton-Fronlenac):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this resolution reverses the flight of time for me some 18 years or so back to 1937, when I had occasion to speak on a similar resolution. As the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has just stated, the resolution for national scholarships had at that time been introduced by the then member for Essex East, who still has the honour to represent-and ably represent-this same constituency in the person of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin).

The resolution of 18 years ago was very well presented, and the expose that the sponsor made at the time fully outlined the needs as well as the possible consequences of putting the resolution into effect. Since that time similar resolutions have been introduced into this house, predicated always on the beneficial results which would be derived nationally by the implementation of its subject matter. Although 18 years have passed since the first resolution was introduced by the hon. member for Essex East in 1937, we have had this afternoon positive and tangible evidence of another very able presentation of the subject matter of the present debate, by the hon. member for York Centre, who introduced the resolution. I wish to congratulate him on his speech this afternoon on national scholarships, and his invitation, especially to the members from Quebec, to take part in this discussion is the reason why I am only too glad to support the resolution presented to us by him.

It is patent to us all that the purpose of the resolution is to supplement, if possible, the educational efforts not only of the federal and provincial governments but of all existing organizations interested in the subject of education.

Education is a heritage that we ourselves in this generation must assist in every possible way so that, as we pass from the field of activity, we shall leave behind us those who are probably better educated than we have had an opportunity of being. The resolution also means a greater use of our educational system and making of that system a greater national asset and a greater national benefit.
That there is often financial embarrassment to many of our students cannot be gainsaid.

It we take into consideration the fact that 44 per cent of the children of the country issue from 14 per cent only of Canadian families, the assistance which can be given to needy students is recognized by all of us as one of the best investments a country can make.

In 1948-49, when university enrolment in the country had reached the total of 80,000, 30 per cent were ex-servicemen holding bursaries from the federal government. Apart from ex-servicemen, only one out of six or seven students in Canada, or less than 14 per cent of the total enrolment in Canadian universities, were holders of scholarships, even when participants in vocational training schemes were included.
In 1938, 14 per cent of Canadian students were scholarship holders. It must therefore be admitted that we have not made very much permanent advance in the 10 years from 1938 to 1948.

On the other hand, in Great Britain, in 1947, 25 per cent of the students, apart from ex-servicemen, held bursaries. Present government plans in Great Britain will result in the increase of this proportion to 70 per cent of the total number of university students. In the United States, 20 per cent of university students are on scholarships.

The report of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences mentions that 143 briefs had been presented to it up to 1950, and among these were those presented by the National Conference of Canadian Universities, the Trades and Labour Congress, the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour, and the Professional Institute of the Civil Service of Canada.
All of this goes to show the very high importance of the matter of education in the view of Canadians.

It is admitted by almost each and every one of us that, in accordance with the confederation act, education is under provincial jurisdiction. In no way must this requisite be interfered with, and at all times must this precept be adhered to.

I have been impressed this afternoon by the declaration of the hon. member for York Centre of the very small percentage of financial grants affecting students directly, out of the total grants made. I am wondering whether the matter could not be gone into with a view to increasing that percentage of only 6 or 7 per cent-if I recall correctly-that directly affects the students.
I know that it behooves each and every one of us to do all we can to increase, whenever it is possible to do so, the assistance for

needy and worthy students. I am wondering also whether some of our industries could not do a little more than they have done in the past in the establishment of scholarships particularly for worthy needy students. Corporation profits in 1954, for example, totalled $1,800 million. The figure for 1955 is estimated to be over $2i billion, an increase in profits of over $400 million in the last year. Surely here is a splendid opportunity for the corporations of Canada to lend their assistance to the establishment of national scholarships. In doing so they will not only assist needy students but will also assist themselves at the same time to secure the scientists and technical men they will need in the future.

The great need is for first-class men to give leadership and inspiration through their own brilliant, original discoveries. The future depends not only on the continued liberality of government agencies but on the number and quality of the men induced to do research work. The greatest need is to discover and train these men, and surely the resolution of the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) will, if implemented, assist us to attain the aim envisaged.

,Liberal,,Joseph-Adéodat Blanchette,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=86cdb90c-8049-4642-8b59-ba1d2f99d892&Language=E&Section=ALL
1824605,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.20,1956-01-26,eb20cb84-344e-40aa-b7af-f2a7ff88f1f5,ca.m.9512,Mr. G. H. Casfleden (Yorkton):,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to enter this debate and with the assistance of one of the cabinet ministers to have on record the very important fact that this matter has been before parliament for about 18 years. My plea this evening is simply that we have a change from words to cabinet action. I regret, and I am sure we all do, that the resolution does not come from a cabinet minister as it would then be the prelude to a bill which would do something about the matter. In the time I have been in the house I have read a number of copious commission reports. I could refer to the Massey commission which was set up to find out what should be done in Canada to assist in the development of the intellectual resources of our country having in mind the keeping in Canada of young men trained in our universities instead of watching them migrate in their thousands to the big country to the south of us.

I want to congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) on adopting this great cause. I wish him well, and I can guarantee him support similar to what he has had from all the opposition. I hope he can convince the cabinet that something should be done about the matter.

I could not speak tonight without paying tribute to the member from the university city of my own province, the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), who spoke so ably this afternoon and who for years has sponsored the cause of education of Canadian

youth and university training. I want also to congratulate the Canadian university students association on the work they have done in contacting members of the house and asking them to support the resolution by letting the government know that by and large the Canadian people are solidly behind something being done at this time.

I do not suppose any teacher in Canada could fail to be moved by the shocking waste of some of the finest intellects that enter our public schools, a waste brought about because of poverty, with the result that these young people are not able to take higher education and some of the brightest minds of our country are lost to the nation. This has been a matter of concern to me ever since I was a student in high school. I will never forget the plea expressed in Thomas Gray's ""Elegy in a Country Churchyard"" where, referring to the graves of the people from that rural area, he said:
But knowledge to their eyes her ample page
Rich with the spoils of time did ne'er unroll;
Chill penury repress'd their noble rage,
And froze the genial current of the soul.
Full many a gem of purest ray serene
The dark unfathom'd caves of ocean bear:
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen,
And waste its sweetness on the desert air.

The time has come for Canada to stop wasting these gems of intellect, these flowers of beauty. Today the world is changing very rapidly. It is more evident than ever that no nation can hope to rise in the scale of peoples unless it maintains the highest possible training of the greatest number of its people who are capable of taking university training and benefiting from it. Scientific and cultural advances are made in the world today at breathtaking speed, and the very existence of our nation depends more and more on our ability to train the intellect of our youth.

A few years ago, when more opportunities were available, young people could earn enough to put themselves through universities much more easily than they can today. The resolution of the Canadian university students association, forwarded by the students' representative council of the University of Saskatchewan, draws this fact to the attention of hon. members in these words:
Whereas there are many university students in real need of financial assistance;
And whereas still more persons anxious to attend university are prevented from doing so by financial necessity;
And whereas the cost of attending university has been rising more rapidly than the earning power of students;
And whereas assistance available to Canadian students compares unfavourably with that available in other countries;
And whereas it is a loss to our Canadian social, cultural and professional life as well as to the
individual concerned whenever anyone abandons or does not enter university for financial reasons;
Be it resolved that the students' representative council of the University of Saskatchewan;

column2: Supports the current national student campaign for increased and more numerous government scholarships and bursaries.

column1: They also go on to say:
In view of the urgency of this situation, specific and immediate governmental action should be taken to provide such scholarships.

They do not need to urge the members of this group to support such a resolution. Every year we lose thousands of university students and many university graduates to the United States. Surely that is a sign that we in Canada are not providing opportunities for them within our own country. The development of the natural resources of this country should be the job of the young people whose minds have been trained in Canada. Can we not provide that opportunity here? The time is long past when effective action should have been taken by the government with regard to this matter.

I support the idea put forward this evening by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) with respect to the provision of a revolving fund. Many students would welcome the opportunity to take advantage of a revolving fund program under which they could borrow money to attend university. After they had graduated they could then make use of their higher earning power to repay the money to the fund in order to assist other students in the same way.

There is one thing, however, that we must all face and that is the question of educational facilities in Canada today. If we are going to have more students in our universities then it is quite evident to anyone who has surveyed the situation at all, that Canada needs additional university facilities most urgently. Dr. Sidney E. Smith points out that we are very inadequately equipped even for the 65,000 students who are attending our universities today. The problems facing our universities are most serious; they are inescapable and imminent. The trouble is that the basis of support of our universities is entirely inadequate. It is a matter of serious national dimensions which cannot be overcome and remedied without government assistance on the national level. As a nation we dare not neglect this matter. As a parliament, we are each and all responsible fqf immediate action in Canada on this matter.

Modern society is making greatly increased demands on the universities. Obviously those demands can be fulfilled only if society is willing to meet the demands of the universities. The universities just cannot exist, Ie1 alone expand, on ""good will and fair words"",

This problem is bigger than this government appears to realize. It is the present government that is responsible. Action is urgently needed. Surely the word of the greatest experts in education in the dominion should be taken when they put forward such reports as we find in the Toronto University monthly of January 1956. Every recent report on higher education throughout the country stresses this point-indicating that a matter that previously was sponsored just as a good cause today has become one of national necessity. From a federal government point of view, our record in this field is pitiable. In view of the national importance of the matter, I think the record is just one of complete neglect. I regret exceedingly that there has been no evidence of federal action at the cabinet level before this time.

I take great pleasure in supporting this resolution. I only hope that what has been said here today will be a step forward in convincing the cabinet of Canada that the Canadian people are aware of this extremely important and imminent problem. It is their responsibility to act on it now.

1824609,ca.proc.d.1956-01-26.29.1.24,1956-01-26,6ffdccf5-fe20-4be5-b99d-1593863458ac,ca.m.1985,Mr. Hellyer:,,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,,Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure for me to support this resolution sponsored by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth). He is to be commended for his initiative and for the considerable research which was necessary in the preparation of his opening address.

In November, 1954, the students administrative council of the University of Toronto invited all members of parliament for the Toronto metropolitan area to attend a meeting sponsored by that council for the purpose of seeking support for increased and more numerous government scholarships and bursaries for Canadian students. The meeting was well attended. The hon. member for York Centre was there, as were the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) and many others. It was ably presided over
by Mr. William Angus, who occupied the chair. Mr. Angus at that time was president of the students administrative council.

I should like to mention a few of the points that were contained in their brief. The first point they mentioned was that there are a substantial number of Canadians who are qualified to obtain higher education and who do not obtain it because they lack the necessary means. From my own personal experience, Mr. Speaker, I know of a number of people in my year at school who were unable to proceed beyond the high school level and to take university training simply because their parents did not have the financial means necessary to support them.

Canada lags far behind other countries, particularly the United Kingdom, in the amount of assistance provided students. If the twentieth century is truly to belong to Canada we must overtake other countries in this field. As was mentioned earlier, the Russian government is sponsoring many scholarships, particularly in the sciences, in the hope of graduating a sufficient number of engineers to overtake us in technology. We must do everything possible to make sure that we keep up to, and indeed ahead of them in every field.
A university education is increasingly necessary to any sort of personal advancement. It therefore must be freely available if the best qualified are to hold the key position in Canadian society.

A bursary scheme of this kind would aid in recruiting older students with work experience who add greatly to a university, as was shown by the D.V.A. experience. I was one of those people who were fortunate enough to receive government assistance after the war. I feel that it is my responsibility and duty to do anything I can to obtain the same assistance for others. The benefits conferred on this country by this program are so great as to be difficult to calculate.
Such a program would be broad enough to assist the valuable ""good"" all-round student as well as the merely brilliant one.
Mr. Speaker, may I move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Hellyer the debate was adjourned.
